author: Alex Salmon
title: The absent history of social upheaval after WWI
content:
Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I By Fiona Skyring Perth: UWA Press November, 2025 225pp RRP $39.99

Peace Day celebrations were held across Australia on November 14, 1918, following the end of World War I.

Even though the shooting had barely ended, the social tensions created by the war would be exposed in riots and brawls involving returned soldiers in Adelaide, Broken Hill and Townsville. These were predecessors to the riots that occurred from 1919–21.

Author and historian Fiona Skyring explores this history in her 2025 book, Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I.

In Townsville and Broken-Hill, riots and brawls occurred between self-styled “loyalist” soldiers and trade unionists, socialists and anti-conscriptionists. In Adelaide, soldiers showed their support to striking tram drivers, 300 of whom had served in the Australian Imperial Forces (AIF), by organising and attacking strikebreakers.

The Australia that WWI soldiers returned to was deeply divided by class, religion, social and political issues. The country had been rocked by the 1916–17 anti-conscription referenda, the 1917 New South Wales general strike, and international events such as 1916 Irish Easter Uprising, the 1917 Russian Revolution and the 1918–19 influenza pandemic.

In 1918–19 these divisions continued, as the country experienced a cost-of-living crisis, which was compounded by the mass bereavement due to the war.

Industrial upheaval continued in 1919 with 6.3 million days lost to industrial action, figures unmatched even in the 1970s. The largest strike was waged by the Seamen’s Union, which shut down wharves across the country between May and August.

In Riots, Skyring examines the way the ANZAC legend was being constructed by writers such as Charles Edwin Woodrow Bean, even as WWI continued.

In Bean’s ANZAC Book, published in 1916, the stories of soldiers who said they didn’t want to fight, thought their comrades’ deaths were futile and felt the class divisions between officers and ordinary soldiers in the AIF, were excluded.

Bean wrote in 1919: “Australia (has become) a new nation. Five years ago, the world barely knew her. Today, the men who went to fight for her have placed her high in the world’s regard.”

The celebrated legend of the ANZAC was dominated by the ideal of the overwhelmingly white, tough man from the bush; a classless citizen soldier whose sacrifice was made in the name of nation, empire and freedom. This narrative excluded the 1000 Aboriginal men who served in the AIF and who would experience more discrimination upon their return after the war’s end.

The message that civilian society should honour the soldiers’ sacrifice and any criticism of WWI being seen as “an attack on the soldiers” made it easy for right-wing politicians, industrialists and organisations such as the Returned Soldiers and Sailors Imperial League of Australia (RSSILA) to paint anti-war activists, trade unionists, socialists, Irish republicans and members of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) as “disloyal”.

When 1000 socialists and members of Brisbane’s Russian exile community carried red flags on a march through the city in defiance of the 1914 War Precautions Act, on March 23 1919, the conservative press and other forces in collaboration with military intelligence whipped up xenophobic anti-communist sentiment.

This resulted in a crowd of 7-8000 returned soldiers marching to South Brisbane, attacking the headquarters of the Russian Workers’ Association and engaging in an anti-Russian pogrom. These events became known as the Red Flag Riots.

Further soldier’s riots would occur in Fremantle, Melbourne, Kalgoorlie-Boulder and Sydney between 1919 and 1921. The Sydney 1921 riots inspired D H Lawrence’s 1923 book, Kangaroo.

However, the soldiers’ riots were not all directed against socialists and trade unionists.

Skyring describes the events of November 1918, when returned soldiers acted in solidarity with striking tram drivers in Adelaide by attacking strikebreakers.

Soldiers returning home on a troop ship to Fremantle Port in Western Australia on May 5, 1919, also gave their support to striking lumpers – workers who loaded and unloaded shipping cargo. There are accounts of soldiers fighting with police on Fremantle’s streets, in the days following.

In Melbourne, soldiers fought police for four days straight, in July 1919, over the lack of …

author: Danica Rachel
title: Protest called against October arms fair in Perth
content:
The Land Forces Exposition 2026, to be held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on 6-8 October, will be a three-day extravaganza of exhibitions, talks and luncheons, where the main topic of conversation is how best to kill people. More than 20,000 weapons company executives, politicians and military personnel from around the world are expected to attend.

We have to protest against this outrageous celebration of death and destruction.

Photos from the 2024 event on the front page of the

Land Forces website

 are enough to make you ill. A smiling representative of Anduril, a company specialising in AI-powered warfare, shows off a battle drone. A live demonstration of a robot dog, presumably designed to carry autonomous weapons, takes place on the exhibition floor. A drone as big as a car hangs from the ceiling.

Lockheed Martin, the world’s biggest arms dealer—and builder of the F-35 fighter jets Israel uses to bomb Gaza—will have its latest death machines on display. As will Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons company.

Senior executives from Anduril and BAE Systems will speak on a panel discussing “the realities of Ukraine, Iran and other current conflicts”. Today’s bloodshed used as a case study to make tomorrow’s killing more efficient. What could those “other conflicts” be? Israel’s invasion of Lebanon? One assumes that there’s much these monsters have learned from Gaza, too.

Lockheed Martin and BAE will be joined by Babcock, Boeing, Honeywell, Northrop Grumman and Thales. Aside from all having had significant roles in providing Israel’s weapons for use in Gaza, they are all on the exclusive list of companies involved in creating nuclear weapons.

The list goes on, and on, and on. More than 650 companies will have exhibits on the floor, all of them dealing in weapons, military hardware or AI systems for warfare.

To say the state Labor government is rolling out the red carpet for this smorgasbord of warmongers would be an understatement. It is going above and beyond to keep conference-goers comfortable by pouring $11.5 million into security.

Special legislation gives police the power to set up checkpoints, stop and search anyone for any reason, and ban anyone they like from a significant section of Perth’s CBD, including a major train and bus station, for ten days surrounding the event.

Police Minister Reece Whitby said of the laws: “We saw the scenes that occurred when Land Forces was held in Melbourne in 2024, and we do not want to see anything like that here in Perth”. Whitby was referring to the

protest by 1,500 people

 against the last iteration of this festival of death.

None of this—the war profiteering, the authoritarian police powers, the increased drive towards a world of total war—should pass without protest.

So a coalition of anti-war and Palestine solidarity organisations has called a demonstration against Land Forces on 6 October, 5pm, at Yagan Square in the Perth CBD. We need as many people as possible to make it clear that we reject Land Forces and everything it represents.

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists’ election campaign in full swing
content:
The Victorian state election will take place in just over two months, on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Socialists’ campaign is now in full swing, with local campaign activity taking place daily across Melbourne and regional Victoria.

The scale of the campaign—with VS candidates set to run in all 88 lower house seats and all eight upper house regions across Victoria—is beyond anything the socialist left in Australia has attempted for generations (if ever). Even just a few years ago, a statewide campaign like this would have been unthinkable. That it’s happening at all is something of a breakthrough.

Between 1 June and 19 September, VS volunteers knocked on more than 80,000 doors, already well on track to reach the 2022 campaign total of around 190,000. The party received around 2,000 requests for campaign signs to be put on front fences and in yards, eclipsing the 2022 total of 1,000, with hundreds of orders a week still coming in. More than 2,400 people donated to the campaign, and almost 1,800 registered for a party event. 

New branches are springing up everywhere. Wherever they do, we’re finding people who want to get involved. VS events in places like Pakenham, a suburb on the far south-eastern fringe of Melbourne—more than 50 kilometres from the CBD—are attracting many new faces. And we now have active branches in regional centres including Geelong, Warrnambool, Ballarat and Bendigo, and the beginnings of branches in Shepparton, Wodonga and Warragul. 

We’re accustomed to being almost completely overlooked by the mainstream media, but the sheer size of our campaign this time means we’re increasingly difficult to ignore.

ABC News reported

 on the VS campaign launch on 1 August, and Channel 9 reported on our “all-in” Footscray doorknock on Sunday 16 August, which was attended by more than 350 volunteers. VS candidate for the Northern Metro upper house region Omar Hassan has become something of a regular fixture on talkback radio 3AW’s morning show with Tom Elliot—most recently on the topic

“what is socialism?”

VS candidates in the regions are attracting particular attention.

Hera Sheppard,

 in the seat of

South-West Coast

 (comprising Warrnambool, Port Fairy, Portland and surrounds), has been featured in several articles in the

Warrnambool Standard

, including the front cover. An

article at ABC News

 and an appearance on ABC Radio followed—the latter

drawing the ire

 of Australia’s richest billionaire Gina Rinehart, who objected to Hera’s claim that she was pushing for Australians to work for $2 a day (in the 2012 quote Hera referenced, Rinehart worried about Australia’s competitiveness when “Africans want to work, and its workers are willing to work for less than $2 per day”). It certainly helps that, at 18, Hera is one of the youngest candidates ever to run for parliament in Australia, but regional media in general have shown a keen interest in VS candidates everywhere. 

Signs also suggest the campaign is resonating. In Footscray, where VS volunteers have already knocked on around 17,000 doors, and the campaign has put up more than 200 yard signs, a steady trickle of people have turned up to volunteer at the campaign office after receiving VS material.

There’s no escaping the fact that politics in Victoria has shifted decisively to the right, and it’s likely either a Liberal or a Liberal-One Nation Coalition government will be elected on 28 November. But there’s no shortage of people who are horrified by the rise of One Nation and who are relieved to find, when visited by a VS volunteer, that there’s a party offering a genuinely anti-establishment alternative on the left. 

Hassan tells the story of Mary, an 82-year-old he met while doorknocking in the outer northern suburb of Thomastown. A long-time Labor voter, Mary told Omar that she wouldn’t vote for the ALP this time because “they’ve completely lost their way”. He later recounted:

She described playing with all the Italian and Yugoslav kids, going to each other’s houses and having great fun. ‘It made life richer, having all the different cultures, growing up together’.

title: Errico Malatesta – Vote? What For?
content:
George: This beer’s not too bad, is it?

Jack: Yes, it’s alright, but what a price!

George: Shocking – especially when you remember what things used to cost. Still, you can’t wonder with all these taxes. It costs you twice as much to live as it used to. They put up the price of some things, and say you can do without them. But you can’t do without bread, and food, and clothes – you have to pay the rent all the same, and then there are the taxes on this and the rates – on our wages too! What a life! And it’s our own fault! If we wanted to we could alter things. The working class has the remedy in its own hands.

George: Easy enough! You’ve got a vote?

Jack: What’s that got to do with it?

George: Have you, or haven’t you?

Jack: Well, I’m entitled to a vote – but I never make use of it.

George: There you are! You’ve got a vote, but you just won’t take the trouble to use it, and then you wonder why things are so bad. You deserve all you get, honestly! People like you are responsible for all the trouble in the world!

Jack: Alright, alright, keep your hair on! Just tell me what’s the good of voting?

George: It’s obvious. Who makes the laws? The M.P.’s. Elect good M.P.’s and you get good laws.

Jack: Good councillors and good M.P.’s? We’ve heard that for a long time. But you’d have to be deaf, dumb, and blind not to notice it’s the same stooges that always get in. Oh, it’s wonderful to hear them when they’re after votes at election time. They pat you on the back, ask after the wife and kids, kiss the baby, promise you railways, bridges, work, cheap bread, less taxes, higher wages, protection – absolutely everything! And once they get in, they’re no better than anyone else. Goodbye promises! The wife and kids may starve, there’s no more or less work than before, the whole town can be falling to pieces for all they care. They’ve other things to think about than your troubles! Then a few years later they start the ballyhoo again. It doesn’t matter what colour the party is: they’re all the same. As soon as they’re elected, they forget all about you. They’re in their clubs and at their select dinners, and they don’t even trouble to come and have a look at you until the next election.

George: That’s correct! But why elect the rich? Don’t you know that the rich only live on the work of the masses? So how do you expect them to worry about the masses? All they think of is getting as much out of the ordinary man as they can.

Jack: Now you’re talking! But it’s not only the rich. There’s the other type, who want to get elected so they can become rich.

George: That’s true. So don’t let’s vote for them. Let’s elect workers, experienced friends of ours, as you might say, and then we won’t be fooled.

Jack: Oh, we’ve got some of your “experienced friends” in now, and they’re no different from our acknowledged enemies! Anyhow, what do you mean, “let’s elect – let’s elect.” As if we – you and me – could do as we like!

George: But it’s not only us two. If each one of us tried to convert other people and they would do the same, labour would have a majority, and we could elect whoever we liked. And that’s when we could form a government of the workers, and then . . .

Jack: And then it would be a paradise – I mean for those who were in Parliament! You’re arranging things a bit too quickly! Those in command always have the majority. The rich are always in power. Just imagine a poor worker, perhaps with an ill wife and four hungry kids, and you tell him to risk his job and get thrown out of his house to starve; just to give his vote to a candidate his master doesn’t like. Just try and convince those poor devils who can be thrown out of work by their boss whenever he likes. They’re never free; if they want to be free, they don’t want to waste their time voting – just take what they need.

George: But if we didn’t do that, no-one would vote. We couldn’t go to the workers and ask them to vote for our party, and say at the same time that votes were useless.

Jack: That’s just it! And on top of that you have to make election promises you know you can’t keep. And then you have to stand in with the Government, and mix with the well-to-do, and all the rest of it. As soon as any of your men are elected they have to kow-tow to the people you admit are the opponents of the workers. So why the hell talk about propaganda when the first thing you do is to counteract propaganda?

George: But you must admit, it’s an advantage to have our own men with …

author: Tom Bramble
title: What’s the deal with productivity?
content:
The bosses are trying to convince workers that lower corporate taxes, fewer regulations and workers’ rights, and less union power would be good for real wages. What they really want is more profits at the expense of the working class.

For years, business lobby groups have decried what they call Australia’s “productivity crisis”. They don’t say workers are producing less than they used to; they say they aren’t increasing production as quickly as before and aren’t keeping pace with overseas productivity growth.

It’s true: growth in workers’ hourly output has slowed over the past decade, and Australian workers don’t produce as much value for the bosses as American workers. But the bosses argue that this means living standards are held back, and prices rise more than they otherwise would, contributing to the cost-of-living crisis.

They say that government regulations (rules about wages, hours of work, health and safety standards, construction standards, environmental protections and professional and occupational registration requirements) and trade unions are preventing business investment. Their solution is “deregulation”, “slashing red tape”, “more competition”. These are simply code words for attacking the working class.

Let’s break this down. First, what is productivity? The simplest definition is “output per hour”. For BlueScope Steel, it could be tonnes of steel produced per hour per worker. For a childcare centre operator, it could be the number of children in care per worker per day. Lift those and productivity rises.

But who benefits? Does the steel worker or childcare worker see their wage rise automatically if they get more done? Of course not. In the first instance, all the money made from extra production by every group of workers goes to the capitalists, not the workers. Workers’ standard of living depends on how much they fight for. And that applies across the whole economy.

The bosses say some of the additional money coming in from workers’ extra effort will come back through higher wages and maybe more jobs. They argue: “a rising tide lifts all boats”. Is that true, though?

First, productivity in Australia may have slowed in the past couple of decades, but it has still risen. Yet household living standards are no higher than they were in 2012. There is no indication that workers are seeing any of the higher value they produce in the form of higher real wages.

A starker example is the United States, which bosses always point to as the high-productivity benchmark, where output per worker is higher and rising faster. In that country, workers’ share of national income is now at its lowest since World War Two—the productivity gains have gone to the capitalists, who have grown ever wealthier at workers’ expense.

Take things down another level. Even if bosses shared a cut of the higher revenue from increased productivity with workers, or unions successfully struck to extract a higher wage, bosses would still be ripping off workers.

All wealth ultimately comes either from the world’s natural resources or from human labour. You only have to see what happens when workers go on strike to see the truth of this—nothing gets produced, not a wheel turns, the childcare centres lie empty. All the machinery, all the factories, all the railway lines can only be put to good use if workers labour on them. And these in turn are the product of previous generations of workers’ labour.

What the capitalists call productivity should really be called exploitation: the extraction of value from the worker over and above the cost of their reproduction, i.e. what is necessary to get them to come to work each day in the form of wages. They call it profit; in fact, it’s theft from the worker.

This theft lies at the heart of capitalism. It explains why the workers labour their whole lives and have not much more than their home to hand on to their kids, and often not even that. While their employer has significantly expanded their operations at the workers’ expense. Some of the bosses may blow the money on a more self-indulgent lifestyle, but personal greed doesn’t get to the heart of it.

Every boss is driven to extract more from their workers, i.e. to lift productivity, because if they don’t, their rivals will, and they will be undercut and go out of business. The winner is the boss who can exploit their workers the most. That’s why every boss in every country demands that governments make it easier for them to rip off their …

author: Brian Mahony
title: Coffs Harbour council rescinds climate emergency declaration
content:
Coffs Harbour City Council voted 4–3 on September 24 to rescind its 2022 declaration of a climate emergency.

The motion was put by Mayor Nikki Williams, who also sought to remove Scope 3 emissions from the council’s Renewal Energy and Emissions Reduction Plan (REERP) and delay accepting the plan for several months.

Williams stood as an independent, but local media has reported that she is a member of the National Party.

Greens Councillor Jonathan Cassell, who put the initial climate emergency motion in 2022, said council had “smash[ed] climate action in our council for the foreseeable future”.

“Climate inaction is costing us more and more, and if we aren’t prepared to act swiftly and urgently to address climate change then we are going to pay more in future.”

The 2022 motion passed 5–4, after impassioned speeches from students from local high schools who called for urgent action on climate change.

author: Emma Black
title: Strangulation: How did attempted murder become normal?
content:
A 16-year-old woman from Sydney’s northern beaches died in hospital in late August after reportedly being strangled during consensual sex with her partner. The tragedy has sparked a long-overdue reckoning with the consequences for young women of the pornification of sex and the normalisation of sexual violence that has come with it.

In recent years, sexual strangulation has gone from being a relatively marginal phenomenon to an everyday sexual practice. In Australia, 61 percent of young women report having been strangled during sex, according to a

2024 survey

 of thousands of 18- to 35-year-olds. Men are most likely to be the stranglers. There is no safe way to strangle someone. According to David Corlett and Marie Crabbe, founders of anti-strangulation advocacy group Breathless:

“Potential 

consequences

 [of strangulation]

range from

 neck pain to loss of bladder and bowel control, headaches, memory loss, seizures, brain damage, stroke and, as seems to be the case with the young woman from the northern beaches, death. The risks and consequences are cumulative, so the more someone is strangled, the more likely they are to suffer harm.”

Only a tiny percentage of middle-aged and older adults have engaged in sexual strangulation, but among young people it’s become commonplace. Maree Crabbe, who is also the director of

It’s Time We Talked

, says strangulation wasn’t an issue before about 2019. But things have changed dramatically since then. “In recent years, we’ve been hearing it’s become normal for young people of all backgrounds, socioeconomic groups, cultures, sexual orientations”, she recently told the

Sydney Morning Herald

.

So how did a potentially deadly act become a normal sexual practice?

The main driver is pornography.

Recent research

 found more than 60 percent of 18- to 35-year-olds had encountered sexual strangulation depicted in pornography. One study comparing the content in the most popular pornography across the two and a half decades to 2024 found that sexual strangulation has gone from almost non-existent to featuring in 15 percent of scenes.

Pornography has become the de facto sex education system for millions of young people. And strangulation is just the latest trend in an industry that maximises profits by selling more extreme depictions of violent and degrading treatment of women.

A landmark 2010 study of best-selling pornographic videos, published in the journal

Violence Against Women

, found that 88 percent contained physical aggression, while 49 percent of scenes contained verbal aggression. Perpetrators were usually male, whereas targets were overwhelmingly female. Targets most often showed pleasure or responded neutrally to the aggression.

So the vast majority of mainstream pornography, whether it depicts strangulation or not, reinforces the idea that violence and humiliation are not only permissible, but pleasurable for women. The pornography industry has “blood on its hands” for propagating this sort of violent content, according to Chanel Contos, founder of

Teach Us Consent

.

An example of how normalised strangulation during sex has become came from this year’s Eurovision song contest.

Romania’s 2026 song entry

 “Choke Me” repeats the words “choke me” 30 times in three minutes. The song also contains the lyrics “It’s hard to breathe in” and “make my lungs explode”.

Many mainstream commentators

emphasise

 the importance of avoiding “kink-shaming” when addressing the issue of sexual strangulation with young people. This dresses up the prioritisation of men’s sexual gratification over women’s safety as sex-positive open-mindedness. And it wilfully ignores the fact that sexual desires and practices are not simply a matter of individual preference; they are shaped and constructed in a society where women are not equal to men, and enormous profit can be made from sex by companies competing for market share.

The reality is that people’s sexual inclinations have not radically changed on their own over the last 50 years, such that the majority of men now enjoy inflicting harm on women. Market forces have pushed things in this direction. In an attempt to be more sensational and attract market share, pornography companies have taken the male-dominant trope that underpins the construction of mainstream heterosexuality and pumped it up to a new extreme. This has shaped attitudes to sex and sexual desire, which in turn further reinforces the business model. And …

title: Trabajadores de VW en México podrían declararse en huelga en Octubre.
content:
Trabajadores de Volkswagen en México podrían salir en huelga si no se llega a un acuerdo con la compañía antes del dos de octubre. Los 6,500 trabajadores producen la Jetta, Tiguan y Taos en la planta de Puebla, la instalación más grande de Volkswagen fuera de Alemania. Su sindicato, SITIAVW, es uno de los sindicatos independientes más históricos de México, y está en proceso de una revisión salarial en la planta.


El 11 de septiembre, los trabajadores rechazaron de forma abrumadora la oferta de un aumento combinado del 10 por ciento en salarios y prestaciones. (El sindicato había propuesto un aumento de 17 por ciento anteriormente.) Días antes de que el acuerdo provisional se sometiera a votación, Volkswagen eliminó uno de tres turnos en un segmento de la planta que produce la Jetta y la Tiguan. Aproximadamente

800 trabajadores

 perdieron sus empleos, reporto

El Financiero

.


Dentro de días de los despidos, el sindicato

anuncio

 que 611 de los trabajadores—quienes no firmaron acuerdos de separación—serian elegibles para reinstalacion cuando Volkswagen comienze produccion de su linea Golf en la planta de Puebla en abril. Pero ya era muy tarde: 5,925 de los 6,440 votantes elegibles participaron en el voto de ratificación; de ellos,

73 por ciento votaron para rechazar la oferta

, en lo que asesor de SITIAVW Willebaldo Gómez Zuppa califico como una expresión de indignación por los despidos. El acuerdo también hubiera

pospuesto la siguiente revision salarial

 a un plazo de 18 meses en lugar del ciclo anual.


“No somos ciegos ante la delicada crisis que atraviesa la industria automotriz alemana, ni ignoramos los retos financieros globales que argumenta Volkswagen,”

 dijo el sindicato

 en una declaración despues de que los trabajadores rechazaron la propuesta. “Pero que se escuche claro hasta Wolfsburgo: ¡la crisis de los corporativos no se va a resolver a costa del sudor, los derechos y el futuro de la clase trabajadora mexicana!”


Volkswagen no respondió a las solicitudes de comentarios.


DESPIDOS GLOBALES


En septiembre, VW anunció planes para eliminar

100,000 empleos a nivel global para 2030

—marcando el mayor recorte de empleos visto por un solo fabricante de automoviles. IG Metall, que representa 120,000 trabajadores de Volkswagen en alemania y está en el consejo de supervision de la empresa,

 afirmó al

Guardian

 que ambos lados habian hecho sacrificiso para prevenir “una escalada peligrosa al conflicto.”


No queda claro cuantos recortes más se preveen en Puebla. Desde 2012, la planta ha recortado su plantilla en un 36 por ciento,

reporto

Milenio

, pero continua siendo uno de los empleadores más grandes en el estado hoy. Algo como 6,500 trabajadores de producción se emplean directamente en la planta, que produce vehículos principalmente para la exportación en Estados Unidos. Algunos 30.0000 más trabajan en la cadena de suministro automotriz en el estado.


“Para mí, la explicación: la empresa desde minuto uno nunca quiso negociar,” afirmó Gómez Zuppa. “Lo más rápido que puedes hacer para reducir costos es el despido de trabajadores. Creo que en ese sentido, ellos están buscando un conflicto mayor para tener la justificación de hacer un ajuste de mayores dimensiones.”


Las huelgas en México son diferentes que en Estados Unidos. Bajo la ley laboral mexicana, las compañías deben frenar la producción enteramente en una planta en huelga—a diferencia de lo que ocurre en Estados Unidos, donde las compañías pueden recurrir a gerentes y emplear a trabajadores de reemplazo para continuar con operaciones. Eso le da a los sindicatos mexicanos un enorme poder. Pero las huelgas en la industria automotriz—la séptima más grande del mundo—han sido sumamente escasas en las últimas décadas, ya que la mayoría de contratos colectivos en la industria están en las manos de sindicatos de protección patronal, quienes han sido aliados clave en el modelo de desarrollo mexicano basado en salarios bajos. SITIAVW, uno de los pocos sindicatos independientes, ha ganado los salarios más altos en la industria.


Pero las huelgas si conllevan ciertos riesgos.


En México, los empleadores deben proveer una justificación al gobierno cuando realizan despidos. Entre esas justificaciones pueden figurar las pérdidas ocasionadas por una huelga, señaló Gomez Zuppa: “Abre la posibilidad frente al gobierno de decir, ‘Por eso tengo que despedir a tantos.’”

title: Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στους/τις διωκόμενους/ες από τη παρέμβαση για την απεργία πείνας του Γ. Μιχαηλίδη, Τρίτη 29/9, 09.00 στα Δικαστήρια Λαμίας
content:
Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:


Συλληφθέντα από την παρέμβαση στις 13/6/23 στα δικαστήρια Άμφισσας


Δίκη από παρέμβαση στην τελευταία απεργία πείνας του αναρχικού συντρόφου Γ. Μιχαηλίδη


Καλούμε σε συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στο εφετείο Λαμίας, την Τρίτη 29/9/26, στις 9πμ


Τα καλοκαίρια του 2022 και του 2023 σημαδεύτηκαν από δύο μεγάλες μάχες που έδωσε μέσα από τη φυλακή ο αναρχικός σύντροφος Γιάννης Μιχαηλίδης.

Με κύριο αίτημα την αποφυλάκισή του

, που το κράτος εκδικητικά του αρνούνταν παρά τα χρόνια που ο σύντροφος είχε ήδη εκτίσει,

ο Γ.Μ. προχώρησε στην αναβαθμισμένη επιλογή των απεργιών πείνας

, φτάνοντας και τις δύο φορές σε οριακή κατάσταση υγείας. Την 30η μέρα κατά τη δεύτερη απεργία πείνας πήρε την απόφαση να κλιμακώσει και με απεργία δίψας, που είχε τελικά ως αποτέλεσμα τη νίκη του αγώνα του και την απελευθέρωση του συντρόφου.


Στη μάχη αυτή, ο αναρχικός χώρος στήριξε τον αγώνα του απεργού, καλώντας κεντρικές συνελεύσεις που διεξάγονταν πολλές φορές ανά βδομάδα, παράγοντας λόγο και δράσεις σε πανελλαδικό επίπεδο. Στην Αθήνα, το κίνημα αλληλεγγύης, από διαφορετικά μετερίζια αγώνα, προσπάθησε με όλες του τις δυνάμεις να δείξει την αλληλεγγύη του πολύμορφα στον αγώνα που έδινε ο σύντροφος. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό έδρασε και

η “Συνέλευση αλληλεγγύης στον αναρχικό απεργό πείνας Γιάννη Μιχαηλίδη”

 η οποία επιχείρησε να κεντρικοποιήσει το ζήτημα, να το ανοίξει κοινωνικά και να αναδείξει την εκδικητικότητα του κράτους απέναντι στους πολιτικούς κρατούμενους καθώς και να ασκήσει πίεση στο κράτος ώστε

να αποτρέψει τη δολοφονία του συντρόφου

.


Μία από τις παρεμβάσεις της συνέλευσης, που έλαβε χώρα στις 13/6/2023, ήταν η ανάδειξη της ευθύνης των δικαστικών αρχών που κρατούσαν τη ζωή του απεργού στα χέρια τους

. Των δικαστών της Άμφισσας δηλαδή, οι οποίοι, σε ευθυγράμμιση με την κρατική στρατηγική, καθυστερούσαν επί μήνες τις διαδικασίες αποφυλάκισής του μη εξετάζοντας καν το αίτημά του. Με την υγεία του απεργού να βρίσκεται λοιπόν σε οριακή κατάσταση, έχοντας ήδη ξεκινήσει και την απεργία δίψας,

πέντε συντρόφισσες και σύντροφοι της συνέλευσης

 πήγαμε στην Άμφισσα, όπου και

πραγματοποιήσαμε παρέμβαση με σπρέυ και τρικάκια στα τοπικά δικαστήρια που αναδείκνυαν την κρατική και δικαστική δολοφονία του συντρόφου μας

.


Αφού πραγματοποιήθηκε η παρέμβαση,κατά την αποχώρηση μας, μπάτσοι της περιοχή μας συνέλαβαν. Μετά από λίγες ώρες, βρεθήκαμε στα δικαστήρια της Άμφισσας, όπου περάσαμε από εισαγγελέα,στην οποία δηλώσαμε τους λόγους της παρέμβασης μας, με εκείνη να ειρωνεύεται τον απεργό πείνας Γ. Μιχαηλίδη και “προετοιμάζοντας” μας για την επερχόμενη καταδίκη μας.

Στο δικαστήριο που ακολούθησε, τονίσαμε την οριακή κατάσταση της υγείας του συντρόφου μας, το ιστορικό βάρος της ενδεχόμενης δολοφονίας του και την ευθύνη που φέρει το κράτος και ειδικότερα οι δικαστές της Άμφισσας

. Υπερασπιστήκαμε τον απεργό πείνας και τον αγώνα που έδινε βάζοντας ανάχωμα το ίδιο του σώμα διεκδικώντας την απελευθέρωση του. Τέλος, αναδείξαμε τη σημαντικότητα της αλληλεγγύης προς τους πολιτικούς κρατούμενους και τη συνολική εναντίωσή μας στον θεσμό της φυλακής. Καταδικαστήκαμε για διακεκριμένη φθορά και απείθεια λόγω άρνησης δακτυλοσκόπισης χωρίς εκπροσώπηση δικηγόρου.


Οι ποινές που μας αποδόθηκαν ήταν 30 μήνες φυλάκισης με αναστολή και 3.600€ χρηματική ποινή στο καθένα μας

. Τόσο το ύψος των ποινών, όσο και το μεγάλο χρηματικό ποσό που μας επιβλήθηκε, αναδεικνύουν την εκδικητική μεταχείριση μας από το δικαστήριο.


Αντιλαμβανόμαστε την αλληλεγγύη στους αγώνες των φυλακισμένων ως αναπόσπαστο κομμάτι των αγώνων που δίνουμε ενάντια σε κράτος και εξουσία.

Τις ιδέες και τα προτάγματά μας θα τα υπερασπιστούμε και στο εφετείο, που θα πραγματοποιηθεί στις 29 Σεπτεμβρίου 2026 στην Λαμία

, στοχεύοντας παράλληλα να περιοριστεί όσο το δυνατόν περισσότερο η έκδηλη εκδικητικότητα των πρωτόδικων ποινών.

title: Labour department warns JNU management over non-compliance of orders, demands immediate cessation of layoffs and abuse of contract employees
content:
After over 1200 workers at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) threatened to go on strike on 28 September 2026 over alleged exploitation and labour code violations, a hearing overseen by a labour department conciliator has led to the management being warned over “legal implications” of repeated violations of binding labour agreements, and issued orders for immediate provision of safety equipment to workers, halting layoffs, constituting a Grievance Redressal Committee, and more. The strike has been called off for the time being under the assurance of the management’s future compliance.


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


New Delhi, 28 September 2026:

 In the matter of an industrial dispute between the contract workers of Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, represented by the All India General Kamgar Union and the university as well as private middle-man firms through which over 1200 of the university’s employees are contracted, a hearing on 25 September 2026 overseen by labour department conciliator Vinay Rana has led to stern warnings for the university and private firm managements over non-compliance with several labour laws, as well as directions for immediate rectification.


 


As per the 25 September settlement, the AIGKU, on 11 September 2026, served a notice to the university Registrar and Vice Chancellor announcing a contract workers’ strike on 28 September 2026 in pursuance of eight demands. These demands sought the rectification of various alleged labour-code violations by employers that jeopardised workers’ safety, made their employment financially exploitative and precarious, and undermined their rights and working conditions. The eight violations enlisted were as follows:


 


Non-payment of minimum wages on account of alleged manipulation of attendance.


Non-grant of earned leave and casual leave and uncompensated work on gazetted holidays.


Non-payment of statutory bonus with arrears for three years.


Augmentation of manpower in view of increased workload.


Unfair labour practices against workers and union office bearers.


Termination of contract workers engaged in hostel housekeeping and mess work with effect from August and September 2026.


Non-issuance of wage slips, identity cards, protective equipment, second uniform to security guards and non-display of statutory notices.


Illegal deductions, unilateral punishment of security guards and non-constitution of the Grievance Redressal Committee.


 


Copies of the notice were, as per the settlement, endorsed to the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi, and the Secretary, Ministry of Labour and Employment. The notice was then forwarded to the second Assistant Labour Commissioner,

named


Devendra Kumar Ram on the Labour Department website, in the office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) in Dwarka Sector 10. It was received on 24 September 2026, and the conciliation meeting overseen by Rana was held there the following day.


 


JNU is the principal employer responsible for the welfare of the aggrieved employees, but like most disputes in the contracting era, not the sole one. Two private security firms, Rakshak Securitas Pvt. Ltd. and A.E. Securitas Security and Allied Services (the security contractors of the university), along with Q Group (contractors of housekeeping staff in the university hostels) and Max Maintenance Services Pvt. Ltd. (contractors of maintenance staff) were also named.


 


Such conciliation proceedings take place in industrial disputes under Section 53 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.


 


AIGKU was represented by its President, Sucheta De, along with State Secretary of the All India Central Council of Trade Unions (AICCTU, which is a major Indian trade union affiliated with the CPI(ML) Liberation), Surya Prakash (State Secretary, AICCTU), Vice President of AIGKU’s JNU unit, Surya Prakash, and a member of AIGKU’s Executive Council, Manikant Patel.


 


JNU was represented by its Deputy Registrar and Labour Welfare Officer Abhishek Kumar Singh; Section Officer (Legal) Vineet Kumar Bizenia; “Assitant Admin (sic)” Imran Kataria; Sanitation Inspector Saurabh Kumar and Data Entry Operator Sandeep Kumar. None of the private contracting firms showed up to the meeting, despite being called upon by the authorised conciliator to appear and present written submissions and relevant employment records.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Contract nurse questions workers’ compensation denial after she was hit by ATV
content:
A nurse who was struck by an ATV this summer in Gjoa Haven says she won’t return to Nunavut because she feels unsupported by the territorial government and

Workers’ Safety and Compensation Commission.


Teresa Vo uses a walker during rehabilitation at West Park Healthcare Centre in Toronto in July. She is now an outpatient at the health centre. (Photo by Sam Laskaris, special to Nunatsiaq News)


Teresa Vo was in the middle of a four-week nursing contract when she was

walking home

 from a late shift at the hamlet’s health centre on June 18. A child driving an ATV struck her, leaving her with multiple fractures and internal injuries.


She is still in physiotherapy, limited in how far she can walk and unsure when she will be able to work again.


While in recovery, Vo fought a second battle over whether the accident happened during “the Course of Employment” — a technical determination on which thousands of dollars of workers’ compensation payments hinged.


“Dealing with this, feeling like I’ve been thrown under the bus and having to figure all this out on my own, is quite daunting,” she said.


Vo said her nursing contracts did not tell her that an injury while walking between her employer-provided accommodation and her work might not be covered. She also said

she has not received return-to-work support from the GN, such as disability support she received from another employer in the south.


“I believe there is a broader issue here about how remote and northern health-care workers are protected, supported and treated when something goes seriously wrong,” Vo said.


Claim denied, then accepted … then denied again


The Workers’ Safety and Compensation Commission first denied Vo’s claim on July 24. She appealed on Aug. 6, which the commission accepted.


The commission

 paid out $3,783.89 on Sept. 2 for two weeks of missed work.


Then, on Sept. 3, the commission overturned its decision again, citing information provided by the GN, and Vo was asked to repay the money she had received.


The commission sent her another letter on Sept. 17, saying it wouldn’t attempt to recover that initial payment. (WSCC does not recover payments it made if “a previous compensation decision is changed.”)


The claim denial cited a policy that says since Vo

was not on employer premises, no work incident had occurred and the injury did not arise out of and during the course of employment.


Vo disputes this because she was a travelling nurse, living at employer-provided accommodations, and had no other reasonable option to get home. 


She had worked overtime on the night of the incident until about 7:30 p.m. and, because she was not on call, said she could not use one of the two vehicles reserved for nurses who might need to return to the health centre quickly.


She was also unable to hitch a ride with the two other nurses on duty.


Travel insurance helped cover costs associated with her treatment and return south, while Ontario’s public health insurance covered her eligible medical care in Ontario, Vo said.


She hoped WSCC compensation would replace lost income and help pay her mortgage, bills and day-to-day expenses while she cannot work.


‘Employer has a responsibility,’ say labour experts


Christopher McLeod, a University of British Columbia professor and director of the Partnership for Work, Health and Safety, said workers’ compensation systems have traditionally drawn a line between the workplace and a worker’s commute. But that line is more grey in Vo’s case.


“If she was at employer-provided accommodation and going back and forth between her place of work and her accommodation, I think you can make a really strong argument that the employer has a responsibility to ensure that she can get home safely,” McLeod said.


The commission acknowledged the limited infrastructure in Gjoa Haven but said she had completed her shift, was travelling home for personal purposes, was not on call and was not performing work-related duties. Transportation to and from work was not part of Vo’s contract and she was expected to walk, the denial said. Taxis were available if she was uncomfortable walking.


“At the time of the accident, I was travelling directly from my workplace to employer-provided accommodation. This was not an ordinary commute from work to my personal residence,” Vo said in her Aug. 6 email that appealed the decision.


“Taxi service was unreliable to the point that it could not reasonably be depended upon, leaving …

author: Unknown
title: [Nantes / Saint-Nazaire] Histoire de luttes ouvrières de l'été 1955
content:
Extraits des écrits de Nicolas Faucier, ouvrier mécanicien anarcho-syndicaliste Nazairien contributeur au journal Le Libertaire, retranscrits par des militant-e-s de Saint-Nazaire.


En 1955, les chantiers de l'Atlantique groupent sous une seule direction plus de 10 000 ouvriers et employés. Ceux-ci avaient calculé que, tandis que l'indice des salaires était passé de 100 à 548 (de 1946 à 1955), celui des dividendes avait bondi de 100 à 3502.


Les raisons de la colère


"C'est surtout l'année 1955 qui allait témoigner de la tradition de combativité des ouvriers nazairiens engagés dans une action revendicative enfin victorieuse qui mérite qu'on s'attarde quelque peu à en décrire les phases principales. Il importe, auparavant, d'indiquer que, pour passer ainsi à l'offensive avec le maximum de chances de réussite, un travail sérieux de préparation des esprits avait été entrepris par les trois organisations syndicales, réunissant les ouvriers, atelier par atelier, pour les amener à se ressaisir et les convaincre de cesser de rechercher une amélioration pécuniaire à coups d'heures supplémentaires dont la pratique ruinait l'avancement de toute action revendicative du salaire horaire. [...]


Dans les chantiers, en mars et avril, tandis que les négociations avaient repris, l'impatience gagnait, l'agitation s'amplifiait : débrayages quotidiens dans les ateliers, grèves de 24 heures comme le 7 avril, à la

SNCASO

 (aviation) dont les ouvriers rejoignaient ceux des chantiers dans une même manifestation de rue pour gagner la population à leurs légitimes exigences. Défilé impressionnant et inhabituel de 12000 travailleurs envahissant la chaussée, sans pancartes, sans slogans déclamatoires, mais, à l'inverse, silencieux, inquiétant pour le patronat par la ferme volonté qu'on lisait sur les visages de lutter jusqu'au bout pour faire aboutir les revendications. C'est cette volonté qui s'exprimait au meeting suivant la manifestation où la décision fut prise unanimement de continuer l'action par le refus des heures supplémentaires

 

; moyen de pression le plus efficace pour vaincre la résistance patronale obligée de respecter les délais de livraison des pétroliers [...]


À ce moment il eût suffi de peu de choses pour que la violence ouvrière se déchaine. Ce qui eut lieu le 20 juin lorsque les soudeurs, apprenant que leurs bonis avaient été baissés, réduisant leur salaire horaire de 15 à 20 francs, envahirent la direction et ne se retirèrent que sur la promesse de réexamen de leur cas.


Le lendemain matin, n'ayant pas obtenu satisfaction, ils se fâchèrent et appelaient à la rescousse leurs camarades des autres ateliers pour manifester devant la direction qui fut de nouveau occupée. La nouvelle se répandit et, à l'embauche de l'après-midi, la totalité des entreprises de la métallurgie avait débrayé. À l'intérieur des chantiers, l'effervescence grandissant, les ouvriers s'introduisaient dans les bureaux : dossiers, machines à écrire, mobilier volaient par les fenêtres et, malgré les appels au calme des responsables syndicaux, débordés, la direction elle-même était mise à sac et le directeur séquestré [...]


Les responsables syndicaux, bien qu'ayant condamné les excès, en rejetaient la responsabilité sur le patronat qui, méprisant leurs avertissements, croyait pouvoir employer la méthode lui ayant réussi en 1950 et laisser pourrir le mouvement, sans songer que le souvenir de la misère qui avait alors acculé certains au désespoir les amenait, cette fois, à utiliser la violence comme seul moyen d'action capable de faire réfléchir les employeurs et les amener à plus de compréhension.


À 21 heures les ouvriers se disposaient à passer la nuit à la direction avec le directeur retenu prisonnier, refusant de rendre leur otage malgré les objurgations de leurs délégués. Il fallut l'intervention des

CRS

 pour déloger les 200 irréductibles et rendre à la liberté un homme qui pouvait alors méditer sur les inconvénients de mépriser la colère ouvrière trop longtemps contenue [...]


Au cours de la nuit, plusieurs centaines de

CRS

 étaient restées à l'intérieur des chantiers et en gardaient toutes les issues. Ce que constatèrent les ouvriers venus accompagner leurs délégués jusqu'à la grille d'entrée des bureaux qu'entrouvrit devant eux le peloton policier de faction. Pendant que se déroulait l'entrevue, les commentaires allaient leur train contre ces mercenaires du capital, issus de leur classe et grassement rétribués à leurs frais de …

author: By Dingane Xaba, Unicorn Riot
title: South African Graffiti Artists Reflect on Past Present and Future
content:
Durban, South Africa — “In the early days we were painting on two-by-one Masonite boards,” said Iain Robertson, a Durban-based graffiti artist who goes by the name

Ewok

. “That’s how we would do exhibitions as graffiti artists … we’d built our own walls. And this meant that we had to work within quite tight parameters.”


For many years, this was the environment South African graffiti artists had to work under, much of this owing to the generally negative attitudes surrounding graffiti art since its inception in the 1960s. Fast forward to 2026 and societal perceptions around graffiti art have drastically shifted as high-profile art studios and even billion dollar companies have steadily embraced the art form.


South African Graffiti Artist Unveils Anti-Consumerist Mural in Durban


Long gone are the days when graffiti artists were largely viewed as parasites and blights to society. To the contrary, many of those same once ostracized artists have now become revered as cultural icons. Any one living in a major city merely need step outside their door to see the evidence for themselves.


There is no urban environment in the world where graffiti has not made it’s mark. Even in places like Durban — an area mostly known for being the birthplace of Shaka Zulu — there exists a thriving and unique graffiti art community.


History of Graffiti Art and Spread to Africa


The word ‘graffiti’ originates from the Greek word; “graphein,”which means “to write.” The earliest known examples of said art dates back to the stone age illustrated on cave walls in Sulawesi Island, Indonesia. Other well know examples include Aboriginal cave art in current day Australia, as well as the San rock paintings of southern Africa.


Pettakere Cave “Hand print paintings,” the oldest known cave paintings are more than 44,000 years old. [source:

Wikimedia

]


San Bushman rock painting in the Drakensberg. South Africa  [source:

South African history online

]


Aboriginal Rock Art in the caves at Wary Bay, Bigge Island, Kimberley, Western Australia. [source:

John ,Benwell

]


The history of graffiti art in modern times, however, can be traced back to the rise of the hip-hop movement in the late 1960s, with

American artists TAKI 183 and Cornbread being widely recognized as some of the earliest pioneers

.


While most people treat hip-hop as just another word for rap music, in reality rap is just one of the four essential elements of hip-hop culture, the others being breakdancing DJing, and graffiti. Some graffiti legends have rejected this association, countering with the fact that the practice of drawing on walls long predates the advent of hip-hop and that the two cultures are entirely separate.


What can not be debated is that the alliances formed between various graffiti artists, rappers, DJs and breakdancers from the NYC area in the early 70s became the foundation of hip-hop culture. The subsequent boom in popularity of this culture quickly spread across the United States and to the rest of the world, propelling graffiti to international heights.


Cape Town, South Africa


Cape Town was the

first city from which hip-hop

 — and by extension graffiti — was introduced to South Africa. At that time the country was in the final stages of the racist authoritarian apartheid system which had dominated the government for over 50 years.


As well as being a tool for artistic expression, graffiti also became an outlet for young disenfranchised South Africans — in particular the ethnic minority Coloured population — to express their dissatisfaction with the ruling order.

[note: the term ‘Coloured’ refers to a South African multiracial ethnic group primarily made up of mixed European and Indigenous African origin.]


From Cape Town, graffiti steadily made it’s way into the streets of Durban and Johannesburg in the early 90s. It was at this time that Durban-based artists like Tax, Rulez and Ewok began to pick up spray cans and spread their works all throughout the city.


When asked about the origins of graffiti in Durban, Ewok explained that it was essentially via a traveling circuit of Durbanite artists who were inspired by fellow artists in Cape Town and Johannesburg who in turn borrowed heavily from the graffiti scenes in the U.S. and the U.K.


“We traveled to Cape Town, and Johannesburg connecting with other artists there. We would find out what they were doing and we’d literally bring it back here. There was also, at that time, after …

title: La France ne doit pas extrader Gino et Zaid !
content:
Communiqué de l'union régionale parisienne des syndicats

CNT

 à propos des antifascistes Gino et Zaid, menacés d'extradition.


«

 

Non bis in idem.

 

» Derrière cette locution latine se cache un principe essentiel du droit : celui de ne pas être jugé deux fois pour les mêmes faits. Et pourtant la France et l'Allemagne s'apprêtent à piétiner ce principe en revenant sur la décision prise en 2025 de refuser l'extradition vers la Hongrie de Gino, militant antifasciste poursuivi dans le cadre de l'affaire de Budapest.


Chaque année, autour du 11 février, se tient à Budapest la plus grande mobilisation ouvertement néonazie d'Europe. Lors de ce «

 

Jour de l'honneur

 

», des militants en uniformes de différentes milices nazies locales et européennes se rassemblent pour célébrer la résistance de la Waffen-

SS

, de la Wehrmacht, et de l'armée hongroise lors du siège de Budapest par les armées roumaine et soviétique en 1945. Une défaite pour les nazis, qui met fin au massacre des milliers de juifs perpétrés dans la capitale hongroise.


Et chaque année, des mobilisations antifascistes tentent de dénoncer et d'empêcher cette grande rencontre, qui constitue un véritable moment fédérateur pour toute la mouvance néonazie internationale. En février 2023, des affrontements ont eu lieu entre antifascistes et néonazis, certains de ces derniers ayant reçu 5 à 8 jours d'incapacité temporaire de travail. Pour faire exemple, les autorités hongroises, alors menées par le Premier ministre d'extrême-droite Victor Orbán, décident de mettre en place une véritable «

 

chasse à l'homme

 

» contre les militant·es antifascistes. Celle-ci prend la forme d'une campagne médiatique féroce — qualifiant de terroristes les collectifs se revendiquant antifascistes — et de l'émission de mandats d'arrêts européens à l'encontre d'une quinzaine de militant·es, encourant des peines pouvant s'élever jusqu'à 24 années de prison.


Face à l'évidence d'un procès politique, les antifascistes incriminé·es se réfugient à travers toute l'Europe. C'est ainsi que Gino, militant antifasciste italien, se retrouve en France, où il finit par être arrêté en décembre 2024 par la sous direction anti-terroriste alors qu'il se rendait à un match de football. À l'issue d'un long procès, doublé d'une large campagne de soutien mise en place par le Comité Solidarité Budapest et à laquelle l'Union régionale parisienne de la

CNT

 a participé, la justice française a décidé, en avril 2025, de refuser l'extradition du militant vers la Hongrie, estimant que les conditions d'un procès équitable et de conditions de détention respectueuses des droits fondamentaux n'étaient pas assurées par les autorités hongroises.


Cependant, moins d'un mois après ce premier refus sensé enterrer la procédure, c'est au tour de l'Allemagne de demander l'extradition de Gino, sur la base de la même enquête menée par la police hongroise, au prétexte que deux des victimes présumées seraient de nationalité allemande. Et cette fois le 19 août, la même Cour d'appel de Paris décide de retourner sa veste et d'accepter d'extrader Gino, cette fois vers l'Allemagne où il risque jusqu'à 10 ans de prison. Or, on peut légitimement craindre qu'il soit ensuite remis à la Hongrie — qui l'a peut-être déjà condamné en son absence —, l'Allemagne ayant déjà décidé d'extrader illégalement, selon l'aveu même de sa Cour constitutionnelle, la·e militant·e non-binaire Maya vers la Hongrie. Condamné·e en première instance à huit ans de prison, iel y est placé·e à l'isolement, ne bénéficie que d'une heure de sortie et est filmé·e 24h sur 24h.


Le 30 septembre prochain, la Cour de cassation peut encore renoncer à cette complicité de la France dans cette chasse à l'homme. De même, le 7 octobre, la Cour d'appel de Paris peut refuser l'extradition directe vers la Hongrie de Zaïd, militant antifasciste syrien et résident allemand, lui aussi mis en cause dans cette affaire. L'Union régionale parisienne des syndicats

CNT

 réaffirme son soutien à tou·tes les militant·es antifascistes persécuté·es dans le cadre de cette affaire, énième précédent inquiétant de criminalisation politique de l'antifascisme. À travers Gino, Zaïd, Maja, les autres inculpé·es de Budapest mais aussi de Lyon, c'est nous toutes et tous qui sommes visé·es.


Solidarité antifasciste internationale

 

!

The spectre of capitalist culture haunts even revolutionary organizations. During the French May ’68 uprising, a famous slogan stated: “Kill the cop in your head.” Fascism did not disappear in 1945, it merely was smashed from its molar form towards its molecular form, dispersed among institutions.

The archetype of authority, who monitors behaviour and doles out punishment or bestows praise, is embedded deep in the psyche of the individual. The entirety of society is regimented alongside lines of micro-fascistic mechanisms of power. Radical French political philosopher, Félix Guattari saw it as “The power of the bourgeois State, the power of any kind of bureaucracy, the power of academia, familial power, phallocratic power in male/female relationships, or even the repressive power of the super-ego over the individual” all stand ordered alongside order-giving and order-taking lines.

A particle of Hitler is within us each, threatening to burst forward, to assemble into a machine of genocidal monstrosity.

The State, the courts and the prisons, schools, trade unions, the universities and student unions, at the top of each stands a boss, the head looking down at the membership, the spine of the organisation. The institution is the Law, the sadist, wielding its cruel, cold and calculated power that it has amassed due to the hierarchical nature of its structure. It is herein that the anarchist critique of formal, hierarchical revolutionary organisations is borne out.

In 1934, when the German National Socialists emerged victorious, having crushed all opposition, held its massive Nuremberg rally attended by 700,000 party members, as chronicled in Leni Riefenstahl’s 1935 propaganda film, Triumph of the Will. Standing atop a majestic podium, Hitler speaks to a crowd of workers, in total domination over them. One by one, they shout out their birthplaces and skills and affirm their solidarity with the regime.

They stand ready to construct the Third Reich, Hitler its head, the people its spine. Will had indeed triumphed, where libidinal energies are concentrated upon a singular despotic investment which then sprawls across society. The swastika is hung from each building, curriculum is re-designed, the camps are being built and the uniforms recast, language altered, war-industry regenerated, draping the nation in pursuit of the Führer-signifier, death-spiraling towards self-annihilation.

This is not so different from the modern Leninist cult, at the head of which stands the Theorist, who substitutes reality for their own words, and establishes anew a despotic investment, albeit this time it is draped in the ghost of Lenin. Modelled on the Bolsheviks top-down structure, an anachronistic Politburo entrenches itself as the central committee, establishing a bureaucratic inertia which festers the solidification of internal party despotism. title: Jorge Macri disputa el voto a LLA actuando contra los sectores populares
content:
El Gobierno de la Ciudad envió un protocolo que obliga a las directoras a denunciar a estudiantes que “podrían estar cometiendo un delito”. Mientras presiona a juezas por televisión y militariza los barrios, ahora Macri quiere que las escuelas sean prisiones.


Jorge Macri, Javier Milei y Patricia Bullrich. Foto: GCBA


Por Mario Hernandez


En una clara persecución a los jóvenes y una medida casi fascista, el gobierno de la Ciudad envió un protocolo a las escuelas que obliga a las conducciones de las escuelas a denunciar a estudiantes que “podrían estar cometiendo un delito”.


La circular llegó a las escuelas de parte de la Ministra de Educación porteña, Mercedes Miguel para informar sobre cómo aplicar el nuevo Régimen Penal Juvenil en las escuelas de la Ciudad. Régimen por el cual se aprobó la imputabilidad a los 14 años.


En el comienzo del mensaje que llegó por correo electrónico, Miguel informa cómo va a actuar desde el Ministerio para “resguardar la vida escolar y el bienestar de nuestras escuelas”. En lugar de fortalecer los equipos de orientación escolar para contener los graves problemas sociales de los jóvenes Jorge Macri a través de su ministra en Educación les declara la guerra a las principales víctimas de sus políticas que nada tienen que envidiarle a las de Milei.


Desde la agrupación 9 de abril advierten que es “un paso más en la confirmación de un estado policíaco que Macri está imponiendo a la Ciudad”. Además, militarizando los barrios y reprimiendo como se vio en el operativo Tormenta Negra.


Operativo “Tormenta Negra II”

 


Vecinos y vecinas de los barrios denunciaron el secuestro de mercaderías y pertenencias como materiales de construcción, colchones y carros por parte de Espacio Público, también la detención ilegal y al boleo de vecinos y trabajadores. Desde las villas 1.11.14, 21-24 y la 31 (entre otras) llegaron las primeras denuncias y videos.


Alejandrina Barry, legisladora porteña con mandato cumplido por el PTS en el FITU y con una trayectoria de casi 20 años como operadora social en la 21-24, respondió duramente al cinismo de Jorge Macri y su “ley y orden”.


Desde la Coordinadora contra los Desalojos y por la Vivienda Digna que vienen enfrentando los desalojos ilegales de Jorge Macri y su ladero “el desalojador” Walter Gómez Diz tambien criticaron fuertemente el operativo. “Repudiamos enérgicamente a estos gobiernos hambreadores y enemigos de los laburantes y la gente humilde. El mismo gobierno que en las calles de la Ciudad arremete contra vendedores ambulantes, jubilados, docentes y toda aquella organización de los de abajo. Ya les demostramos con una enorme Marcha de la Bronca que fuimos miles los que salimos a la calle. Repudiamos y nos solidarizamos con lxs vecinos del @movdevillasybarriospopulares”, replicaron en su comunicado.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Docentes de la 9 de Abril – Corriente Nacional (@9deabril.docentes)


Docentes, trabajadores de la salud y vecinos cortaron la calle en repudio al operativo en la 21-24


Después de ver cómo sus alumnos llegaban al colegio espantados por el operativo policial de la noche anterior, organizaron junto a trabajadores del Cesac y vecinos cortar la calle Iriarte en las inmediaciones del barrio para repudiar la escalada represiva de Jorge Macri contra los sectores más abandonados por el Estado.


En la tarde noche del jueves, de forma intempestiva se dieron operativos en 15 barrios y villas porteñas, entre ellas la 21-24. Con un despliegue de saturación policial, Jorge Macri reeditó el operativo Tormenta Negra del pasado 15 de mayo. Con policías de la Ciudad, Infantería, helicópteros, motos, cuatriciclos y camiones jaula durante horas montaron su show represivo el mismo día en que el Indec publicaba que 1 de cada 3 habitantes es pobre en la Argentina de Milei. Esa fue la respuesta del Macri para los vecinos y vecinas de los barrios populares al hambre, endeudamiento, precariedad laboral y estructural que sufren.


Federico Puy, docente de una de las escuelas del barrio, integrante del Consejo Directivo de Ademys, estuvo a la cabeza de organizar esta acción de repudio que debe multiplicarse. Junto a otros docentes, trabajadores de la salud y vecinos del barrio realizaron un semaforazo sobre el cruce de la avenida General Iriarte e Iguazú en el barrio de Barracas, a metros del acceso a la 21-24.

title: Karasu: Rıza Altun’s struggle will always guide us
content:
Rıza Altun, one of the leading cadres of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement, and those who lost their lives in the Freedom Movement’s struggle were commemorated at an event held in Paris.


In a video message to the commemoration, KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu spoke about Rıza Altun’s activities from the early years of his involvement in the struggle until his death. Karasu said that Altun assumed responsibilities in various areas of the Freedom Movement, from organizing work in Ankara’s Tuzluçayır neighborhood to Antep, from resistance in prison to his activities in Kurdistan and diplomatic work, highlighting his qualities as an organizer and activist.


Karasu also saluted commemorations for the martyrs that have been held in many cities across Kurdistan over the past month after the announcement of their deaths. He said that the public’s participation in and support for these commemorations had given them great morale.


The message sent by KCK Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu to the commemoration in the French capital is as follows:


“I greet all our people who have gathered to commemorate Comrade Rıza. This is the seventh anniversary of Comrade Rıza’s death. Comrades Baz and Garzan, together with Comrade Rıza, lost their lives in an airstrike on September 25, 2019.


As we remember these comrades, commemorations for the martyrs have been taking place across Kurdistan for the past month. Once again, I remember all those martyrs with respect and gratitude. I also commend our people who have participated in these commemorations with great enthusiasm.


Comrade Rıza holds an important place in the history of our party. He was one of the first cadres of our struggle. Our movement was a group that emerged among university students in Ankara and initially organized within the university youth.


The Apoists were organized among university students in Ankara. They also organized in Tuzluçayır, a neighborhood in Ankara known as ‘Little Moscow.’ Comrade Rıza was the leading figure in organizing the Apoist group in Tuzluçayır.


Comrade Rıza organized dozens of young people and brought them into the struggle. It was him who secured Tuzluçayır’s support for our movement. Just as he brought many young people from Tuzluçayır into our struggle, he also involved his entire family in it from the very beginning. His family became part of the struggle as well. Indeed, one of his brothers and two of his nephews lost their lives in this struggle. In this respect, his family stands among the foremost examples in the history of our struggle and our movement of families who participated collectively.


This in itself demonstrated what kind of militant Comrade Rıza was and what kind of Apoist he was. Because he believed deeply in this struggle and devoted himself to it completely, his entire family also became involved and took part in the struggle, and young members of the family lost their lives.


Comrade Rıza and I went to Kurdistan toward the end of 1976, more precisely, at the end of the summer. We went to Kurdistan at almost the same time. A month earlier, I had gone to Antep with Doğan Kılıçkaya, a valued militant from Tuzluçayır who later lost his life and whose nom de guerre was Yasin. A month later, Comrade Rıza also came to Antep.


At that time, Antep was one of the first places where our struggle developed and became most influential. Comrade Rıza played a very important role in this. While our struggle in Antep developed into a major struggle against fascists, a party culture also emerged there under the leadership of Comrade Haki. Comrade Rıza also played a role in shaping this party culture.


Comrade Rıza was truly known as a militant within the struggle. He was an important and influential militant of the Apoist group. He was very composed and highly effective in the struggle against fascists. While he was in Ankara, in Tuzluçayır, he also waged a significant struggle against fascists. During his struggle there, Comrade Rıza’s code name was ‘Şirket’ (‘Company’). He was given this name because of his organizational abilities.


In Tuzluçayır, a truly effective struggle was waged against fascists under Şirket’s leadership. Comrade Rıza was not only an influential militant in our freedom movement’s struggle against fascists, but also served on the first military council of our movement. Together with Comrade Mehmet Karasungur, he was a member of the military council.

title: APPEL A MANIFESTATION ANTIFA LE 10 OCTOBRE - AIX EN PROVENCE
content:
A l'appel de Aix Antifa et d'autres signataires comme Tsedek, UJFP, UPM, LFI, AfroQueer Révolutionnaires, Aix Vanguard,Extinction Rebellion et le Collectif Antifasciste Sud Luberon, toustes solidaires pour dire NON à L'extreme droite


10 OCTOBRE — 11H FAISONS FRONT CONTRE L'EXTRÊME DROITE


L'extrême droite avance mais nous ne la laisserons pas passer. À l'approche des élections présidentielles, le rassemblement national progresse et se trouve aujourd'hui en tête de nombreuses intentions de vote. Cette progression doit nous alerter et nous pousser à construire dès maintenant une riposte populaire, sociale, antiraciste et antifasciste. Car derrière les sondages, il y a la réalité du racisme et des discours de haine qui se banalisent L'extrême droite se nourrit de la division et de la désignation de boucs émissaires : les immigré·es, les personnes racisées, les musulman·es, les habitant·es des quartiers populaires sont constamment désigné·es comme responsables. L'islamophobie s'installe dans le débat public et nourrit un climat de stigmatisation et d'exclusion. Les personnes LGBTQIA+, et particulièrement les personnes trans, sont elles aussi au cœur d'une offensive réactionnaire. Leurs droits, leur dignité et leur place dans la société sont attaqués. Nous sommes dans une période où le néonazisme se banalise et progresse : de plus en plus, des personnes se sentent suffisamment à l'aise pour afficher ouvertement des symboles et des saluts nazis dans l'espace public. Cette banalisation doit nous faire réagir : nous ne pouvons pas laisser la haine et les idéologies fascistes s'installer comme une normalité.


L'EXTRÊME DROITE N'EST PAS INVINCIBLE


Elle cherche à nous convaincre que sa victoire serait inévitable. Ce n'est pas le cas. Nous refusons que le racisme, l'islamophobie, la transphobie et la haine deviennent la norme. Et nous refusons que la colère contre la précarité, les bas salaires, les services publics détruits et les inégalités soit tournée contre celles et ceux qui en sont aussi victimes.


NOUS VOULONS UNE AUTRE FORCE


Un antifascisme populaire et antiraciste qui rassemble largement et s'organise dans la durée. Car l'extrême droite n'est pas invincible. Il est possible de repousser l'extrême droite par notre mobilisation. L'année dernière, c'est cette mobilisation syndicale et populaire qui a permis d'empêcher que le gala du réactionnaire Stérin se déroule au 6MIC. C'est aussi la mobilisation qui a permis de faire partir le pseudo « journal » raciste Frontières du campus aixois. Chaque fois que nous sommes nombreux·ses, organisés et solidaires, nous pouvons faire reculer l'extrême droite. Le 10 octobre, faisons de la rue un espace de résistance et de rassemblement.
