title: Donald Trump and the Age of Evil
content:
By any standard of morality, Trump is depraved. But adorned with the power of the state, he descends to another level — the level of evil.


 


CHRIS HEDGES


25 SEP, 2026


 


Donald Trump exhibits the classic traits of psychopaths — superficial charm, grandiosity and self-importance, need for constant stimulation, a penchant for lying, deception and manipulation and incapacity for remorse or guilt.


 


But is he evil?


 


If, as the philosopher Susan Nieman

writes

, evil is not simply the opposite of good but inimical to it, if the aim of evil is to destroy all moral distinctions, then Trump qualifies as evil. Morality, for Trump, is for losers. All life is transactional. Self-interest and self-enrichment usurp all other considerations. No one else matters.


 


In her new

book

, “Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era,” Neiman argues that evil “isn’t cruelty but something much worse: the ideas that allow cruelty to become ordinary.”


 


She continues:


 


There’s a difference between calling one action evil and calling another a crime. Crimes are things for which we have procedures—at least for punishing, if not for preventing. This means that a crime can be fit in some way into the rest of our experience. To call an action evil is to suggest it cannot—and that it thereby threatens the trust in the world that we need to navigate it. There’s no signpost on the border between evil and awful. Evil is what you say when your jaw begins to drop if you sense that a line has been crossed.


 


Trump crosses line after line. He

declares

 wars on a whim. He

enriches

 himself and his family in crypto schemes, from which he has made over a billion dollars. He orders

assassinations

 and the

kidnapping

 of heads of state. He uses billions of taxpayer dollars to sustain genocide in Palestine and since January 2025 has

provided

 over $20 billion in new arms sales to Israel. He

guts

 government departments designed to lift up the vulnerable and

bloats

 the war budget. He builds

rogue

 paramilitary forces to terrorize citizens and immigrants. He attacks and attempts to

censor

 the news industry.


 


In short, he does what all who commit evil do.


 


He fosters a world where nothing is sacred and where democracy and civic virtues do not exist.


 


Concepts of fairness, decorum, justice and empathy are imploded by the Trump administration. His

threat

 to annihilate Iran – i.e. carry out genocide – announced of all places at the United Nations, is greeted with indifference by a public rendered numb by his moral vacuity.


 


“Once the supremacy of self-interest is enshrined as commonsense realism rather than a philosophical idea, moral capacities like empathy and shame become not just naïve but suspect,” Neiman writes. “Sadists exist and cause no end of pain. But the most common forms of evil arise from the view that only fools believe in anything but their own advantage.”


 


The institutions designed to protect democracy, to safeguard civic virtues, to foster equality — including the courts, law firms, universities and the media, all of which have been captured by the billionaire class — swiftly fell to their knees to curry favor with the Trump White House. The titans in Silicon Valley

showered

 him and his campaign with millions of dollars. The supposed virtues these institutions and individuals claimed they championed were jettisoned. These virtues, they illustrated, were nothing more than branding, performance art, a sham.


 


To an enraged public Trump’s transparent greed and cruelty is preferable to the slick hypocrisy of the politicians, Republican and Democrat, who preceded him. He does not engage in their faux empathy. In fact, he seems incapable of empathy.


 


Once morality is for fools, virtue makes no sense. Once we believe we should grab what we can, even at the expense of those around us, we surrender to evil.


 


“Unlike the rest of us, he permanently exhibits the combination of motives we are told are the true forces driving human behavior,” Neiman writes of Trump:


 


Nor does he appear to understand any other. Though he recognizes that other people, aka losers, have norms, he has no idea of how norms work, moving people to override self-interest in order to honor them. In acting on the international stage like Richard Dawkins’s ruthless genes, he has attracted millions of followers who tell us they admire his authenticity. This doesn’t mean his followers …

content:
Dossier


Der

faschistische brasilianische Präsidentschaftskandidat

title: Bundesverfassungsgericht setzt Beugehaft aus: Antifaschistin Lina ist frei
content:
Bundesverfassungsgericht setzt Beugehaft aus: Antifaschistin Lina ist frei


Nach mehr als zweieinhalb Monaten endete die Erzwingungshaft gegen Lina per Gerichtsurteil: Am 23. September 2026 hob das Bundesverfassungsgericht die Beugehaft gegen die Antifaschistin mittels einer einstweiligen Anordnung vorläufig auf. Damit beendete das höchste Gericht die willkürliche sechsmonatige Freiheitsentziehung, mit der das Oberlandesgericht (

OLG

) Dresden die Aktivistin für ihre Aussageverweigerung bestraft hatte. In seiner Entscheidung verwies das Bundesverfassungsgericht auf den hohen Wert des Rechts, sich nicht selbst belasten zu müssen, weshalb Lina jetzt bis zur eigentlichen Entscheidung über die eingereichte Verfassungsbeschwerde frei ist.

Vorausgegangen war eine Vorladung als Zeugin im aktuellen Antifa-Großprozess vor dem

OLG

 Dresden am 30. Juni 2026. Lina hatte konsequent die Aussage verweigert und dabei auch auf die Möglichkeit verwiesen, sich selbst zu belasten. Noch vor Ort ließ das Oberlandesgericht (

OLG

) Dresden die Antifaschistin für sechs Monate in Beugehaft nehmen und schöpfte damit das maximal zulässige Höchstmaß der Freiheitsentziehung aus. Mit diesem „Ordnungsmittel“ sollen Zeug*innen genötigt werden, im Prozess die vom Gericht gewünschten Aussagen zu machen.

Bereits im Oktober 2025 hatte das Amtsgericht Dresden sechsmonatige Beugehaft gegen Lina verhängt, die jedoch nicht unmittelbar vollstreckt wurde. Gegen diese doppelte Nutzung des schweren Zwangsmittels war Linas Verteidigung juristisch vorgegangen, doch am 18. Juni 2026 hatte der Bundesgerichtshof (

BGH

) die erneute Verhängung bestätigt und damit den Weg für den inflationären Einsatz von Beugehaft geebnet. Erst die jetzige Beschwerde vor dem Bundesverfassungsgericht hatte Erfolg: Mit dem heutigen Beschluss erkannte der höchste deutsche Gerichtshof die grundlegende Bedeutung der Selbstbelastungsfreiheit an, also des Rechts, sich nicht selbst belasten zu müssen. Dieses Prinzip habe elementare Bedeutung für die Menschenwürde und die Rechtsstaatlichkeit. Deshalb wurde die Beugehaft bis zur endgültigen Entscheidung über die Verfassungsbeschwerde ausgesetzt.

Lina war nach mehrjähriger Untersuchungshaft am 31. Mai 2023 vom Oberlandesgericht Dresden wegen körperlicher Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis und des staatlichen Konstrukts der „kriminellen Vereinigung“ zu fünf Jahren und drei Monaten Haft verurteilt worden. Dieser Prozess war der Auftakt zu weiteren Prozessen, unter denen das derzeitige Dresdner Antifa-Großverfahren im Mittelpunkt steht.

Mit der heutigen Entscheidung setzt das Bundesverfassungsgericht ein klares Signal gegen die inflationäre Nutzung der Beugehaft in den aktuellen Antifa-Prozessen. Gegen Antifaschist*innen kommt dieses sonst kaum angewendete Zwangsmittel in den letzten Monaten vermehrt zum Einsatz: Schon am 25. März war im Dresdner Antifa-Großkomplex ein Antifaschist, der gemeinsam mit Lina verurteilt worden war, als Zeuge vorgeladen. Weil auch er die Aussage verweigert hatte, wurde er ebenfalls direkt vor Ort in sechsmonatige Beugehaft genommen. Hingegen hatte Richter Joachim Kubista gegen aussageunwillige Nazi-Zeugen stets nur geringe Ordnungsgelder verhängt.

„Das heutige Urteil des Bundesverfassungsgerichts stellt unmissverständlich klar, dass Grundrechte und rechtsstaatliche Prinzipien wie das Recht, sich nicht selbst belasten zu müssen, auch für Antifaschist*innen gelten. Das Mittel der Freiheitsberaubung, um Zeug*innen zu Aussagen zu zwingen, muss jedoch prinzipiell aufgehoben werden“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Wir freuen uns mit Lina, mit ihrer Familie und ihren Freund*innen und Genoss*innen, dass sie nach über zweieinhalbmonatiger Freiheitsberaubung nun wieder frei ist. Zugleich fordern wir die sofortige Freilassung des Antifaschisten, der bereits seit Ende März ebenfalls rechtswidrig in Beugehaft ist.“ Brückner schloss: „Die Ermittlungsverfahren, Schikanen und Inhaftierungen von Antifaschist*innen müssen enden. Schluss mit der Kriminalisierung – wir sind alle Antifa!“

 


bert


25.9.2026 - 08:48


Pressemitteilung


Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat die Beugehaft gegen Lina vorläufig aufgehoben. Nach mehr als zweieinhalb Monaten kommt die Antifaschistin frei, bis über ihre Verfassungsbeschwerde entschieden ist. Zentral ist dabei das Recht, sich nicht selbst belasten zu müssen.

author: John Mullen
title: Will the French have a fascist president next May? Questions and answers about the far right in France today
content:
The upcoming French presidential election next May carries weight far beyond France’s borders.

A victory for fascist candidate Marine Le Pen — in a major world economy — would embolden far-right movements globally while dealing a terrible blow to French workers, particularly women, LGBT+ people and Muslims.

Conversely, a win for the radical left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, of the France Insoumise (France in Revolt, FI)[1] would offer an important boost to anti-capitalists everywhere.

This election will be anything but business as usual. A recent poll revealed that 71% of voters want the new president to bring about “real social and political change”.[2]

This Q and A aims to explain the key dynamics at work, as well as the strengths and weaknesses of antifascist activity in France today.

Will the French have a fascist president next May?

Nobody can know the answer to this question right now, but the danger is very real. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National (National Rally, RN) is the favourite in the polls, with around 33% of voting intentions for the first round.[3] No other candidate polls above 20%.

Le Pen has particularly gained ground in recent years among women voters[4] and public sector workers, traditionally populations where the left is strong.

A quarter of public sector workers who say they feel close to a political party cite RN as that party.[5]

Worse, polls at present show her winning in the second-round run-off against any other candidate, whether right, centre-left or radical left.[6]

The first round will take place on April 18 next year, with the two leading candidates going on to a run-off on May 2.

In 2022, Emmanuel Macron won the second round by 18.8 million votes, to Le Pen’s 13.3 million.

Importantly, 13 million registered voters stayed home that day, 3 million spoiled their ballots, and another 4 million citizens were not even on the electoral roll.

In the first round, the FI’s Mélenchon secured 7.7 million votes — just 400,000 short of beating Le Pen to the second round.

Unsurprisingly, fatalism is rife in France faced with this historic danger. But Le Pen’s high polling numbers are no reason to despair. The FI has already started a huge campaign to push back against the far right — and this has worked in the past.

Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, 30 consecutive opinion polls predicted that RN would become the largest party in the National Assembly, with several forecasting an absolute majority.[7]Instead, the most dynamic campaign for 50 years, by parties, trade unions and associations of all kinds, along with the alliance of all left-wing parties into the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front, NFP),[8] led to a real victory: the far right came in third in number of seats, behind the NFP in first place and Macron’s coalition in second.

Who are the other candidates? How do the elections work?

The political situation, and the list of candidates, is extremely fluid. For the moment, the rest of the left, outside the FI, is fractured. The Socialist Party (PS), which received only 600 000 votes at the 2022 presidential elections, is a muddle of jockeying wannabes. Five of them will take part in a lacklustre primary mid-October.

The Communist Party (PCF) has decided to stand their own candidate again — Fabien Roussel — with a “class struggle but anti-woke” profile. The Greens leader Marine Tondelier has also announced she is standing. Left-wing loose cannon, the filmmaker and current Deputy, François Ruffin, is already campaigning.

Some of them will give up and support a stronger candidate (sometimes after negotiations concerning the program or support in subsequent legislative elections).

Others will have to give up because they cannot clear the hurdle that the electoral system imposes before a hopeful can get onto the first-round ballot: each candidate must get 500 declarations of support from a pool of 42,000 elected officials (mayors, members of parliament and regional councillors, mostly).

This time around, given the large number of hopefuls, some may not get the 500 endorsements.

The constitution does not allow Macron to stand for a third term, so on the traditional right and in the Macronite neoliberal centre, a number of candidates have emerged — at least five of them. Most are polling quite weakly right now, and some will fold in the coming months.

title: Joint civil society organisations statement on International Safe Abortion Day 2026: Safe abortion is essential healthcare: A call to action
content:
28th September 2026


Joint civil society organisations statement on International Safe Abortion Day 2026: Safe abortion is essential healthcare: A call to action


7 min read


News and Insights


Achieve legal equality


Africa


We join women, girls, and human rights defenders across Africa and the globe on this 28th day of September to commemorate the 2026 International Safe Abortion Day, reaffirming a simple truth: safe abortion is essential healthcare.


We are reminded of the transformative power of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), which is lauded as one of the most progressive and comprehensive legal instruments for the promotion and protection of women’s rights globally, particularly in the area of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). Adopted in 2003 by the African Union, the Protocol goes beyond existing international human rights standards by explicitly articulating a wide array of SRHR protections that are often left ambiguous or unstated in other international and regional human rights instruments.


Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol guarantees women’s rights to health and reproductive autonomy, including the right to control their fertility, decide on family size and spacing, and to choose their method of contraception. Most critically, Article 14 makes the Maputo Protocol the first and only binding international human rights treaty to explicitly guarantee access to safe medical abortion in specific circumstances—namely, where the continued pregnancy endangers the mental or physical health of the mother or the life of the mother or the fetus, or in cases of sexual assault, rape, or incest. This Article also mandates access to comprehensive reproductive health services, including antenatal care, safe delivery, family planning, and sexual and reproductive health education. In doing so, the Protocol moves abortion access from a matter left to state discretion to one of binding treaty obligation — a distinction that remains central to the advocacy for its full domestication across the continent.


Currently, 46 of the 55 African states have ratified the Maputo Protocol, while

nine –  Burundi, Chad, Egypt, Eritrea, Madagascar, Morocco, Niger, Somalia, and Sudan – are yet to ratify it. Bringing these final states on board is vital because over 150 million African women and girls currently live outside the protective legal framework of the Maputo Protocol.


Despite its progressiveness, 9 out of the 46 member states have placed reservations to various provisions of the Maputo Protocol, with Article 14 being the most reserved provision. A reservation lowers the minimum human rights standards contained in a particular treaty for the reserving states and enables the reserving states to escape accountability for

human rights violations

.


Currently, Africa accounts for

70%

of global maternal deaths. These preventable deaths are compounded by persistent gaps in access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) services, which are essential to safeguarding the lives and dignity of

women, children and adolescents

. Unsafe abortions continue to claim the lives of thousands of African women and girls, while millions more are left with severe injuries and long-term health complications. According to the World Health Organization, nearly half of all abortions worldwide are unsafe, with Sub-Saharan Africa carrying the highest burden. The

Guttmacher Institute

 further estimates that three-quarters of all abortions in the region are unsafe, making unsafe abortion one of the leading, and entirely preventable,  causes of maternal death.


The tragedy is not that abortion exists, but that safe abortion is denied or inaccessible. Restrictive laws, vague penal code provisions, and systemic barriers mean that even where abortion is legally permitted, women often cannot access it. The existence of contradictory or vague national laws not only stifles advocacy efforts but also dissuades individuals from seeking or providing (in the case of healthcare workers) necessary health services, as they may fear legal repercussions or stigma. 


By maintaining the reservations to  Article 14 (2) (c), the governments of Mauritius, Kenya, Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, and Uganda deny women and girls access to lifesaving healthcare and perpetuate a cycle of preventable maternal death.

title: Women in Amed call for a united struggle against femicide
content:
Following the femicide of Ayfer Çakmak, women in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) called for a united struggle against patriarchal violence. At the initiative of the DEM Party Women’s Council, numerous women gathered at a busy intersection in the Bağlar district. Ayfer Çakmak, 32, was killed by her husband, O.Ç., on September 25 in the 5 Nisan neighborhood of Bağlar. While the 37-year-old perpetrator was arrested after the killing, the investigation into the femicide is ongoing.


Participants in the rally included DEM Party Women’s Council spokesperson, Halide Türkoğlu, representatives of political parties and women’s organizations, and Amed Co-Mayor Serra Bucak. Ruçem Vefa Elyakut, co-chair of the DBP’s Amed provincial organization, pointed out that women are often killed by men in their immediate surroundings. “Enough is enough. We will not remain silent in the face of these killings,” Elyakut said.


‘Violence against women is a structural problem’


Serra Bucak rejected treating femicides as isolated incidents unrelated to one another. Violence against women is a structural problem and must be addressed accordingly, she said. Bucak particularly criticized shortcomings in the justice system and in the implementation of Law No. 6284 on the protection of women from violence. She noted that municipalities had established various structures to protect women from violence, but could not solve the problem on their own. In this context, she also recalled Rojin Kabaiş and Gülistan Doku. Women and families, she said, must not be left alone in their struggle for truth and justice.


Women are often killed in their own homes


Halide Türkoğlu said that the rally was prompted in particular by the femicide of Ayfer Çakmak, while the protest was also directed against ongoing violence against women as a whole. “Women are being killed precisely in places where they should feel safe, often by the men closest to them. At the same time, women are fighting both male violence and state policies that enabled such violence,” Türkoğlu said.


Türkoğlu stressed that women have the right to live freely and as equals rather than having to fear for their lives. “Can there be a greater disgrace than the murder of a woman?” Türkoğlu asked, stressing that overcoming patriarchal violence cannot be left to women alone. Equality, she added, is a responsibility for society as a whole.


Call to society as a whole


Türkoğlu therefore also addressed men directly, calling on them to take responsibility in the struggle against patriarchal violence. She also appealed to the DEM Party, municipalities, civil society organizations, human rights defenders, shopkeepers, and taxi drivers to join the collective struggle. “Come, let us all take a stand against violence together. Come, let us strengthen this struggle together.”


The rally ended with the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom].

author: David Swanson
title: Parliamentary Dialogue on Peace in Cameroon on the Occasion of International Peace Day 2026
content:
Africa, International Day of Peace, Nonviolent Activism

By Guy Feugap, World BEYOND War’s Africa Organizer, September 27, 2026

On the occasion of the International Day of Peace, celebrated on September 21, 2026, a parliamentary dialogue focused on peace, social cohesion, and the protection of populations was held in Cameroon at the invitation of the United Nations in Cameroon. The meeting, held at the National Assembly headquarters, brought together representatives from Parliament and the Government, civil society organizations, and various stakeholders and partners committed to promoting peace and combating gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Cameroon, already mired in armed conflicts, is now characterized by growing insecurity for people in their daily lives. Unfortunately, institutions have proven unable to prevent and respond to the various forms of violence threatening the population.

The first session of the parliamentary dialogue, dedicated to Parliament’s role in promoting peace, focused on how the National Assembly, the Senate, and members of Parliament can use their constitutional functions and public leadership to contribute to a peaceful environment. Discussions focused in particular on inclusive dialogue, nonviolent political participation, prevention and early warning, accountability in political communication and information, as well as the protection and inclusion of women, youth, people with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups. Peaceful dispute resolution and dialogue were also identified as important elements of peacebuilding.

The second session was devoted to strengthening prevention and response to gender-based violence, femicide, and infanticide. Introduced by the Vice President of the National Assembly and the United Nations Advisor on Peace and Development, among others, the dialogue addressed these forms of violence as issues involving human rights, protection, justice, public health, governance, and peace. The discussions shed light on a troubling situation. The rise in certain forms of crime and violence is an additional cause for concern. Femicide and infanticide—including in places where women and children should be protected, such as homes and schools—illustrate the scale of the challenges facing Cameroonian society. Civil society reaffirmed its role in educating and raising awareness among the public, as well as in advocating for a legal framework to better prevent and punish these crimes. In this regard, World BEYOND War and WILPF Cameroon launched a letter-writing campaign addressed to the Prime Minister, Head of Government, to draw the authorities’ attention to the urgent need for strengthened action against femicides.

On the government’s side, it was noted that the process of drafting the bill on gender-based violence is at an advanced stage and that the text is nearly finalized. Parliamentary representatives, for their part, indicated that they are ready to review and vote on the bill as soon as it is officially submitted to them. This prospect was one of the key takeaways from the dialogue: the need to translate the concerns expressed by civil society and other stakeholders into concrete institutional and legislative measures. Beyond the adoption of a law, the discussions also highlighted the importance of a coordinated response encompassing prevention, reporting, referral of victims and survivors, protection, investigation, prosecution, justice, psychosocial support, and institutional coordination.

The parliamentary dialogue held on International Day of Peace 2026 thus brought together two dimensions that are often addressed separately: peacebuilding and the struggle against gender-based violence. For civil society organizations working on these issues, preventing femicides, infanticides, and other forms of violence is not merely a matter of justice or the protection of human rights. It also contributes to building a peaceful society, in which every person can live free from violence and where institutions fully assume their responsibility to protect. The organizations that participated in this session will continue to ensure that the commitments and discussions arising from this meeting are translated into concrete actions.

Bu süreç sadece bir barış süreci değildir. Aynı zamanda demokratikleşme sürecidir. Bu sürecin karakteri olarak demokratikleşmeyi okuyoruz. O yüzden bu sürecin başarıya ulaşması gerekiyor. Bizim talip olduğumuz, istediğimiz rejimin adı demokratik cumhuriyettir. Demokratik cumhuriyet Kürdün, alevinin, ezilenin eşit şekilde onuruyla yaşadığı bir zemindir, sistemdir. Kayyımların, dil yasaklarının, özgürlüğü kısıtlayan uygulamaların olmadığı bir demokratik cumhuriyet hareketi yaratacağız."

Asgari ücretle insanlar geçinemiyor. Tarımı, hayvancılığı bitirdiniz. DEM Parti olarak çok netiz. Bu düzen böyle gitmez. Bu düzen değişecek.”

title: Kocaeli'de kadın cinayeti: Fatma Çiğil eski eşi tarafından katledildi
content:
Kocaeli'nin Körfez ilçesinde 54 yaşındaki İbrahim Ç. eski eşi 37 yaşındaki Fatma Çiğil'i sokakta ateşli silahla vurdu. Derince Eğitim ve Araştırma Hastanesine kaldırılan yaralı Çiğil müdahalelere rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Yerel basın, Fatma Çiğil'i Vadi Sokak'ta vurduktan sonra olay yerinden kaçan İbrahim Ç.'nin kısa süre önce cezaevinden çıktığını aktardı. Ses Kocaeli'nin haberinde saldırganın daha önce de Körfez Belediyesinde silahlı intihar girişiminde bulunduğu belirtildi.

Polis, cinayeti işleyen İbrahim Ç.'nin bulunması için çalışma başlattı.

Kadın Cinayetlerini Durduracağız Platformu verilerine göre 2026 yılında en az 256 kadın, erkekler tarafından katledildi. Ağustos ayında 22 kadın erkekler tarafından öldürülürken, 33 kadın da şüpheli şekilde ölü bulundu. Ağustos ayında işlenen kadın cinayetlerinden yüzde 64’ünde ateşli silah kullanıldı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Cameron Mitchell
title: ‘No Bystanders’ concert highlights violence against women, raises funds for charities
content:
Caitlin Davies with the support of Australian Femicide Watch, Socialist Alliance, Violent Butterfly Records and other activist groups organised a fundraising concert on September 5 to highlight and educate people about violence against women.

The mixed-bill hardcore concert, titled No Bystanders, heard from 14 local bands, which volunteered to allow ticket proceeds to go to relevant charities.

The all-ages concert included face painting for children and adults, provided by Rhee Brown, and merchandise stalls which lined the Royal Park Hall venue, between two stages.

Each band, hosting several mosh pits, drew an impressive crowd. The energy of the punk/metal music matched the anger felt towards the injustice women face.

The stories of women who have become victim to femicide were highlighted. The wall was filled with faces of women who had been killed by men from 2024 to 2026. The memorial allowed participants to write letters to be read by speakers affected by domestic violence.

Two women, in particular, were the focus of photo collages: Ebony Lee and Ali Lauren. Lee, a close friend of Davies, had her life taken earlier this year. Lauren, a local, was murdered last year by a conspiracy theory podcaster.

Davies said a fundraiser after Lee’s death had raised $46,000 for victims of male violence, and was one of the main inspirations behind No Bystanders.

Violence against women is reaching catastrophic levels. Australian Femicide Watch reports that 49 women and 19 children have been killed by male violence this year, and more than 1300 women and children have been killed since 2000.

Femicide has been exacerbated by the rise of reactionary “manosphere” influencers, such as Andrew Tate, whose profile big tech algorithms push to young men.

Attendees reflected on all the issues at a candlelit vigil towards the end of the night.

Erinn, another volunteer, read Davies’ speech: “We’re standing here surrounded by the faces of women whose lives were taken by violence. They weren't statistics. They were people. They were loved. They had families, friends, futures, whole lives that should never have been cut short. They should still be here.

“A while ago, we lost my two friends, Ebony and Tam, within six months of each other. Their life ended because of a lot of complicated reasons, and so much of that traces back to male violence and the fall-out of it. That kind of harm doesn’t stop in one moment. It keeps moving through people. It affects their mental health, their safety, their relationships, the way they cope, and the weight they have to carry.”

Davies said it is important to stand up against this violence. “What you walk past, you accept. That’s part of why I called this event No Bystanders. Because silence is not neutral. Looking away is not neutral. Grief on its own is not enough. If we actually want things to change, then we have to be willing to look at this clearly, call it what it is, and do something with that.”

The event raised $10,000, of which $8000 was donated to Australian Femicide Watch, and a further $2000 to ERICA Women’s Centre.

Davies told Green Left afterwards that she wanted the event to focus on encouraging young people to recognise the signs of sexual or domestic violence “so that kids can see what toxic relationships can turn into”.

author: Jian Sanz
title: CLSU Student Regent red-tagged in latest attack on student leaders
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Central Luzon State University Student Regent (CLSU SR) Rashela Ballesteros received a package containing red-tagging messages around 12:30 pm on September 17 at the University Supreme Student Council (USSC) office.

The package, sent by a certain Jared Mariano from Guimba, Nueva Ecija, contained a red-tagging message formatted as a love letter, an altered photo showing Ballesteros’s face pasted onto a soldier’s body, and a list of requirements to become an officer in the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). The letter in the package read, “Hope I’ll see your smile in campus.(sic)”

In a statement, Anakbayan CLSU condemned yet another harassment and red-tagging of Ballesteros, reiterating that incidents like these result in serious violations of students’ rights to security and freedom of expression.

“This is a threat not only to SR Ballesteros, but also to the democratic rights of the entire CLSU community. It is crucial to protect the freedom of students to voice their demands and participate in social issues, both inside and outside the university,” the youth organization added.

The organization also compared the tactic to the documented methods used by the AFP and National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) against several student leaders in CLSU. They noted that this incident is a form of surveillance and harassment against Ballesteros, especially since this is reportedly not the first suspicious attempt to contact her.

Related story: Youth groups sound alarm over red-tagging, forced interrogation of student leader

Ballesteros also serves as the national convener of Network Opposed to Pax Silica (NO to Pax Silica), and convener of the Movement Against Destructive Solar Farms (MADSOLAR) and Save the Rice Granary (STRG).

The CLSU University Supreme Student Council (USSC) called the harassment an attack on the broader student masses of CLSU as well. They also noted that the package came months after Ballesteros stood against the continuous cases of surveillance, harassment, red-tagging, and intimidation suffered during the first week of classes in the university.

Since 2024, Ballesteros, fellow student activists and leaders Eyu Bartolome, Cairo Sandoval, and Loi Matias, have faced repeated red-tagging and harassment by military forces and the NTF-ELCAC. Notably, on June 12, 2026, two unidentified men approached CLSU employees to inquire about Ballesteros’s whereabouts.

CLSU USSC also emphasized that despite the university’s formation of a committee addressing red-tagging and attacks on CLSUans, attacks on student activists persist in the university. (RVO)

author: Unknown
title: Rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi sur Frontières queer
content:
Jeudi 15 octobre à 19h30, rencontre avec Sandeep Bakshi pour la sortie de son livre Frontières queer, sexualité, colonialité, décolonialité. La rencontre sera animée par Zaid du collectif sud-asiatique/Brown antiraciste.


Le queer est-il seulement occidental

 

? Conçu au cœur même des Empires, son lexique est-il utile loin des métropoles et logiques coloniales

 

? Dans cet ouvrage, Sandeep Bakshi remet en question les généalogies admises du queer pour échapper aux instrumentalisations et aux normalisations dont il est l'objet.


Partant de pratiques et d'analyses des Suds, ce livre montre que, si les études et le militantisme queer ont produit des formes de pensée radicales, elles ne sont pas immunisées contre les a priori culturels, sociaux et raciaux. Le queer, lui aussi, a sa colonialité. Dès lors, c'est en adoptant une perspective décoloniale que le queer retrouvera toute la vigueur de son insurrection initiale, pour semer à nouveau le trouble.

title: TGEU contributes expertise to new guidance on SOGIE rights in detention
content:
TGEU served on the Expert Advisory Group for the publication Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices, a new guidance note published by the

Association for the Prevention of Torture


(APT). This included providing initial input on the project, reviewing a first draft during a consultation meeting in Geneva in March 2026, and providing expert feedback on an advanced draft.


The publication documents promising practices by governments, prison administrations, staff and oversight bodies to improve conditions for LGBTI people in detention. It pays particular attention to trans communities and highlights approaches that address the structural challenges faced by LGBTI people deprived of liberty.


The publication was presented during a dedicated session at the TGEU Trans Council in Ljubljana on 11 September 2026.

author: Bram Sable-Smith
title: Missouri’s Abortion Rights Face a Second Vote in Two Years
content:
Abortion returns to ballots in Missouri and other states as voters and lawmakers reshape post-Roe policies.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.

Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state’s near-total ban. McCoomb also couldn’t shake the feeling that she’d need to display the sign in her yard again soon.

“I have little faith in our Missouri government,” McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.

Sure enough, just two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3. But while a “yes” vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a “no” vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the “YES” on her yard sign with a “NO” made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.

Voters will weigh in on abortion in Missouri, and three other states, in the November general election. Missouri is also one of two states voting on it for the second time since 2024. Nevada will vote again, too.

The spate of referendums comes after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving each state to make its own abortion policy. The result has been a patchwork of state rules with varying degrees of bans or limitations, and even a series of “shield laws” in states where abortion remains legal that aim to protect providers from prosecution in states where it’s not.

“I just think there’s a constitutional crisis that’s coming,” said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for the anti-abortion organization Students for Life Action.

“Can you have 50 state standards on whether or not a human being is a human being? Can you have 50 state standards on whether human beings have legal protection?” Hamrick said.

That patchwork of abortion protections is the reason Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom introduced the 2024 ballot measure to enshrine the state’s law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception into the state constitution, said Denise Lopez, president of the coalition.

The measure received strong support two years ago, with 64% of voters in favor. Nevada law requires two majority votes to enshrine constitutional amendments, so voters will need to support the expanded protection again in November for it to be enacted.

The Nevada ballot measure wouldn’t change the state’s existing law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception. But the proposal would make it more difficult to overturn abortion access, requiring voter approval of any new ban in two elections.

Lopez said Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom has been campaigning to ensure voters are still mobilized.

“Folks care about it,” she said. “They’re seeing what’s happening at the national level, and they want to make sure that whatever’s happening in our neighboring states, like Idaho and Utah, doesn’t happen here in Nevada.”

Idaho, where a ballot measure establishing abortion rights recently qualified to go before voters in November, has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. Voters will decide whether state statute should allow abortion through fetal viability, the point when a fetus can survive after birth, which is generally considered to be around 24 weeks.

In Utah, abortion is allowed up to 18 weeks while legal challenges to the state’s ban continue.

In Virginia, where abortion is already allowed through two trimesters of pregnancy, until 28 weeks, voters will decide whether to amend their state constitution to codify those rights.

Missouri is the only state voting this year on removing abortion protections already on the books. The measure would repeal the 2024 amendment that guaranteed abortion access through fetal viability in the state and replace it with a ban on abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. author: Isaac Nellist, Chiara Reeves
title: USyd students vote to cut ties with Israel
content:
Students at the University of Sydney (USyd) have overwhelmingly voted for an academic boycott of Israel in a referendum held alongside elections for the Student Representative Council (SRC) over September 22–24.

Honi Soit reported that more than 3500 students, 86% of the 4065 students who voted, were in favour of calling on USyd to adopt an “academic boycott policy against Israeli institutions complicit in apartheid and genocide”.

The referendum motion called on the university to cut ties with Israeli universities, including Tel Aviv University, Technion and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

It also called on management to “end all research partnerships with weapons companies supplying Israel” and for the SRC to “support the struggle for Palestinian freedom”.

All four candidates for SRC President supported the referendum, including incumbent president Grace Street from Grassroots, Emma Searle from Socialist Alternative (SAlt), Ava Cavalerie from National Labor Students (NLS) and Vieve Carnsew from Solidarity.

The referendum was activated by Carnsew and Students Against War/Solidarity after they collected at least 500 signatures.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese gave Carnsew and Solidarity’s “Globalise the Intifada” ticket more coverage by describing it as a “hateful slogan”.

Albanese, NSW Premier Chris Minns and federal Education Minister Jason Clare reportedly contacted university management about the campaign. USyd Vice-Chancellor Mark Scott described the ticket a “psycho social hazard” and banned the ticket from using its signage on parts of the campus.

The Globalise the Intifada ticket said “the smears against our slogan are racist attempts to cover for these crimes that our government and university are complicit in”. “Intifada is the Arabic word for uprising … we are proud to campaign under the slogan. It is a call to end the genocide in Gaza and to free Palestine.”

The referendum result indicates that students support the university taking stronger action to support Palestine and oppose Israel’s genocide.

“Management is attacking the ticket whose members initiated the referendum … this is another blatant attack on the Palestine movement on campus, and an attack on free speech,” Students Against War said on social media.

Honi Soit’s exit polls say Street is likely to win an unprecedented second term as SRC President, collecting 41% of the primary vote. This was followed by Cavalerie (30.5%), Searle (20%) and Carnsew (2.88%).

SAlt won the highest percentage of SRC council votes, with 25%. This was followed by Grassroots (22%), NLS (13%) and PENTA (13%).

Street told Honi Soit that: “Students have said ‘Enough is enough’, that they stand against these oppressive systems and institutions, and that they are fed up with our university’s complicity in apartheid and genocide. We need collective action and a strong student movement, and that’s exactly what students have voted for.”

[Isaac Nellist and Chiara Reeves are students at the University of Sydney. Reeves stood on the Grassroots for Queer Liberation ticket.]

author: Frenny Jowi
title: Congo in Kenya: Why Xenophobia is a Racist Ideal
content:
Thirty-three-year-old Emmanuel is a freelance hairdresser in Nairobi. He is a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in Kenya for six years.


The young man is chic, dressed in designer brands, with a gentle demeanour that reflects his customer-care style in the city’s beauty industry. His calm, collected appearance belies a history of strife, struggle, and an ongoing effort to recover from the decades of armed conflict he witnessed as a child in North Kivu.


‘I will never forget the night when rebels attacked our village in North Kivu. I must have been seven years old at that time. Some people were killed, and there was fire burning everywhere around us.’


Emmanuel narrated his story as he swung around in his styling chair in front of a large mirror that is popularly called a ‘station’ in Nairobi’s hairdressing and beauty salons.


I had visited Emmanuel at the salon where he works. Renting business premises in Nairobi is a significant cost for many young business owners, whether citizen or foreigner. In the beauty industry, most professionals can only afford to rent a mirror and a styling chair as a workstation – hence the name ‘station’.


While occasionally glancing at his WhatsApp notifications for customer bookings, Emmanuel continued to share his story with me.


‘The attack happened many years ago. I still remember how my mother stopped to pack her pot of fish stew and cassava leaves and rice. My father asked her to hurry up, leave the food, and run for safety, but she insisted she would not leave her delicious food. As we all escaped in the dim light of the moon, I recall our neighbours’ comments about my mother’s weird sense of what to salvage. She insisted the food would also save us and she would not leave it behind despite the gunfire. Now I find that funny.’


Emmanuel laughed, trying to find humour in a devastating story.


I knew that talking about traumatic childhood experiences from war would be difficult, so I did not press Emmanuel further about the night armed fighters attacked their village, killing many people and setting houses on fire.


The events Emmanuel witnessed as a child in 2000 were part of the Second Congo War, dubbed Africa’s World War. According to

Amnesty International

, the DRC’s current conflict has been ongoing since the 1990s, particularly in the eastern part of the country, which borders South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania.


This armed conflict escalated in August 1998 when President Laurent Kabila fell out with the Ugandan and Rwandan allies who had helped him seize power.


Emmanuel narrated how the fighting between the Lendu-Ngiti and the opposing Hema began as communal land disputes involving farmers and pastoralists. Locals believe politicians and those with mining interests took advantage of these seemingly solvable disputes to fuel the ongoing war. He added that their radio broadcasts often mentioned various fighting groups such as the UPDF (Uganda People’s Defence Forces) and the UPC (United Congolese Patriots).


‘In the news, when we heard that Bosco Ntaganda was in court and wanted to defend himself in Kinyarwanda, we were all shocked, because locally, we knew him as one of us. We never thought he was from Rwanda. He lived here for so long, spoke our language, looked like one of us, and was always involved in Congolese affairs,’ Emmanuel said.


Decades of conflict have been fuelled by ethnic tensions, political rivalries, corruption, and fighting for control of valuable natural resources.


Over time, the war drew in nine African nations, making it one of the largest wars in African history. The 2017 Kivu Security Tracker Report by Jason Stearns and Christoph Vogel listed 132 armed fighter groups operating in North and South Kivu alone.


Today, Emmanuel is one of the over 100 million citizens of the DRC affected by incessant wars. The DRC is the fourth most populous country in Africa and the 14th in the world. Despite decades of war and pandemics such as Ebola, its population has continued to grow steadily. 


In 2025,

Human Rights Watch

 reported that the Congolese military and a coalition of armed fighters have continued to attack civilians. The report adds that throughout 2024, the

Rwandan

 army and the M23 armed group indiscriminately shelled displacement camps and other densely populated areas near Goma in eastern Congo.


Emmanuel arrived in Kenya in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic. Earlier, in 2017 …

The very concept of race has no biological or genetic validation. It is nothing more than a social construct used as a tool of oppression. The complexity of my individuality can not be represented by “black” identity nor “cultural blackness”. Identities are fixed, generalized representations of people and dictated by social norms, expectations and stereotypes. They are standardized by capitalism and industrial civilization and assumed to be universal and beyond questioning. When I walk into a store I get the stares, all based on the shared concern that I just might steal some shit. But to be honest, they’re probably right. I just might. Because the social placement of my assigned identity is located near the bottom which means my access to resources is limited. author: CMI Argentina
title: Tormenta Negra 2: “no son políticas de prevención del delito, es racismo”
content:
El gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó el jueves 24 un nuevo operativo “Tormenta Negra” en 15 barrios populares con violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. Jorge Macri “consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad” e insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos, denunciaron desde el Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS). “No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad” como Palermo, Caballito o Núñez, señalaron.


Compartimos el comunicado del CELS:


Tormenta Negra 2: el gobierno de CABA entiende a los barrios populares como zonas de ocupación


El gobierno de Jorge Macri volvió a desplegar más de 1500 policías y agentes de control en 15 villas y barrios populares de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. Registramos episodios de violencia policial, detenciones arbitrarias y el retiro de pertenencias y herramientas de trabajo. La CABA consolida una política que identifica pobreza con inseguridad, no con ausencia de derechos.


El jueves 24 de septiembre, el gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizó un nuevo operativo Tormenta Negra en 15 villas y barrios populares. Más de 1500 policías y agentes de control de Espacio Público ingresaron de manera simultánea a los barrios para realizar controles de personas y vehículos, inspeccionar comercios y retirar del espacio público objetos de las personas que viven allí. Es la segunda vez que el gobierno porteño organiza un despliegue de estas características, después del de mayo de este año. Jorge Macri insiste en violentar la vida en los barrios populares y atemorizar a quienes viven en ellos.


Se trata de un modo de entender la ciudad y el derecho a la ciudad con un abordaje racializante y con límites de clase. Es una política que decide qué cuerpos van a ser controlados por la policía, qué familias van a ser desalojadas sin garantías, qué personas deberán demostrar una y otra vez que tienen derecho a quedarse y cuáles tienen que mostrar su documentación en las estaciones de trenes y subtes. La política porteña naturaliza que la principal y primera intervención del Estado en los barrios populares va a ser la policial. Uno de los jóvenes detenidos estaba en situación de calle dentro de la Villa 21. El gobierno llegó con patrulleros, efectivos armados y agentes de control, en lugar de organizar una intervención a partir de las necesidades de quienes viven allí o para garantizar los derechos sobre los que el mismo Estado está en deuda. No hubo presencia de áreas de desarrollo social, sino el despliegue de dispositivos de estigmatización de quienes viven allí, para convertirlos en sujetos de sospecha. El gobierno de la Ciudad abandonó las políticas de integración sociourbana. Ahora se enfoca en una política que niega la ciudadanía de las personas que viven en estos barrios. No existen operativos de este tipo en los otros barrios de la Ciudad, que los invadan a la pesca de ver qué delitos se identifican, que sin duda los hay en Palermo, Caballito o Núñez.


La vara en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires está tan baja que tenemos que reiterar lo obvio: en los barrios populares viven personas que trabajan, estudian, crían a sus hijos que van a la escuela y sostienen redes comunitarias. Tienen derecho a tener políticas que integren las villas con la ciudad en términos de derechos garantizados: a la vivienda, a la salud, a la educación, al trabajo y no estar sujeto a control poblacional permanente. La guerra contra los pobres habla de la pobreza en políticas públicas de la gestión actual de la ciudad. Y del solapamiento de un abordaje que se anuncia como control de actividades delictivas con la persecución de las estrategias de supervivencia. De este modo, la ciudad se fragmenta cada vez más. Los operativos espasmódicos y violentos no llevan orden a estos barrios, sino incertidumbre, abusos y show para las redes sociales. Cuando terminan los operativos y la policía se retira de estos barrios, no permanecen otras políticas públicas.


Durante el operativo del jueves registramos situaciones de violencia policial, uso de gases lacrimógenos y disparos de balas de goma. En la Villa 21-24, los registros audiovisuales que hicieron los mismos vecinos muestran intervenciones contra personas en situación de calle que intentaban resguardar sus colchones y pertenencias. También denunciaron que la policía les sacó herramientas de trabajo. El Ministerio …

author: Unknown
title: Programme d'urgence féministe : 13 mesures contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles
content:
Programme d'Urgence Féministe : treize mesures contre les violences sexistes et sexuelles

 

!


Ce programme n'est qu'une étape pour faire reculer les violences. Les éradiquer totalement ne pourra passer que par le renversement complet du système raciste, patriarcal et capitaliste : par la révolution

 

!


Appropriez-vous ce programme, n'hésitez pas à le diffuser, l'imprimer

 

; tract 4 pages en pièce jointe.


 Article d'origine sur

feministesrevolutionnaires.org


Pour qu'il n'y ait plus aucune violence


Depuis l'irruption de #MeToo en 2017, la question des violences sexistes et sexuelles s'est inscrite durablement parmi les préoccupations majeures de la population. Chaque année, le décompte des féminicides fait la une des journaux. Les dénonciations de violences mettant en cause des figures publiques sont largement médiatisées. Les affaires suscitant l'émotion populaire se succèdent.


En parallèle, on observe un développement rapide des mobilisations féministes, avec des marches massives aux dates emblématiques du 8 mars (journée internationale pour les droits des femmes) et du 25 novembre (journée internationale contre les violences de genre). Bien que ses détracteurs restent très audibles, le mouvement féministe gagne en force et en audience et ses idées et ses discours se diffusent amplement.


Malgré ces éléments favorables,

le mouvement féministe peine à faire émerger des revendications concrètes

 capables d'enrayer à grande échelle les violences sexistes et sexuelles. Pourtant, on ne manque pas de ressources pour comprendre les mécanismes qui permettent les violences. Comment expliquer, alors, que nous ayons tant de mal à y répondre

 

?


Il faut dire que

la tâche est d'une ampleur colossale

 : on estime que près de 280 000 femmes et 160 000 enfants sont victimes de violences chaque année. Et le mouvement féministe se fixe comme objectif, ambitieux, de

réduire ces chiffres à zéro

 

! Or les violences sexistes et sexuelles, au-delà des rapports de pouvoir individuels entre un agresseur et sa victime, contribuent à maintenir l'exploitation des femmes. Par la peur, ces violences disciplinent les femmes et les contraignent à des rôles bien précis dans le système capitaliste : effectuer gratuitement les tâches domestiques au sein de leur foyer, subir des emplois sous-payés dans les secteurs les plus dévalorisés du marché du travail (soin, éducation, entretien…). Pour nous, réduire à zéro les violences sexistes et sexuelles, cela nécessite donc de

transformer radicalement la société en détruisant tout le système patriarcal, raciste et capitaliste : de faire la révolution

.


D'ici là, une série d'étapes intermédiaires peuvent faire baisser les violences. Nous avons tenté de les regrouper dans ce


Programme d'urgence féministe en 13 mesures


. En partant d'une analyse sur les causes des violences, nous déterminons quels leviers il faudrait actionner en priorité pour les faire reculer, et, de là, quelles mesures revendiquer.


La précarité : un accélérateur des violences


Si les violences sexistes et sexuelles existent dans toutes les couches de la société, elles ne touchent pas tout le monde de la même manière. On dit souvent que le viol et l'inceste n'ont ni classe sociale, ni couleur de peau, ni religion. Mais en ce qui concerne les violences conjugales et, dans leur forme la plus extrême, le féminicide, certaines conditions sociales augmentent le risque d'y être exposée.


Les données disponibles suggèrent que

la précarité

,

la dépendance économique

 vis-à-vis d'un conjoint et les inégalités de revenus au sein des couples sont des facteurs qui augmentent significativement le risque d'être victime de violences. Ainsi, dans plus de 80% des cas de féminicides conjugaux en France, les victimes sont soit sans emploi ou retraitées, soit ouvrières ou employées

 [

1

]

]. Les cadres et professions intellectuelles supérieures sont, à l'inverse, très peu représentées. Il existe aussi des corrélations entre les pertes d'emploi, les baisses de revenus et l'augmentation des violences dans les foyers

 [

2

]

].


La conclusion est simple :

la dépendance économique à un conjoint violent est un véritable obstacle à la séparation

, d'autant plus avec des enfants à charge et des aides sociales insuffisantes. Par ailleurs, le motif de la séparation non acceptée est le deuxième mobile invoqué par les hommes qui tuent leur compagne.


La précarité n'est pas qu'une question de catégorie …

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: A Failed Reception System in Crete Turns People on the Move Into Political Targets
content:
Athanatoi, Greece — Residents of a small village in Northern Crete, near Herakleion, are fighting the Greek government’s plan to convert a disused factory into a reception center for people on the move, escalating a monthslong standoff that pits xenophobic backlash against an increasingly securitized European border regime. 


“We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp.” The slogan, painted in red and black across a large banner, hangs from the gate of a factory facing the Candia-Mires state highway, near the village of Athanatoi in northern Crete. A few yards away, a second banner reads: “No camp — the people have a voice.”


A banner reading “We’re not staying silent. We’re not backing down. No to the camp,” hanging from the gate of a factory opposite the abandoned Skouloudis industrial complex. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Across the road stands the disused Skouloudis industrial complex, recently identified by Greece’s Ministry of Migration and Asylum as a site to be converted into a reception center for migrants crossing the stretch of sea between Libya and Greece and landing on the island’s southern coast. Since Minister Thanos Plevris

announced

 the plan in mid-June 2026, Skouloudis has been at the center of a

bitter standoff

 between authorities and local communities.


The former Skouloudis industrial facility, seen from the Heraklion–Mires state highway. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


The choice of this industrial site, however, is only the latest development in a long and contested decision-making process that began in the summer of 2025, when

arrivals in Crete

 far outpaced those recorded along the Aegean route — the sea passage from Turkey to the Greek islands of Lesbos, Samos and Chios that has long been the country’s primary migration corridor — making the island Greece’s main point of entry.


Against a backdrop of chronic absence of adequate first-reception facilities on the island, the handling of landings has fallen to entirely

unsustainable emergency measures

.


The main temporary holding site in Heraklion remains the former psygeio — a Coast Guard cold-storage building in the port area. Meant to hold just 70 to 80 people, the site held more than 450 in the first months of 2026, forcing men, women and children to sleep on the floor.


The lack of adequate sanitation and ventilation created dire health conditions, while pressure to find an alternative mounted further as the Port Authority pursued legal action to clear the site. Faced with this infrastructural collapse, authorities found themselves forced to publicly propose a solution.


One of the rooms inside the temporary first-reception facility known as Psygeio, in the port of Heraklion, where people are held after their arrival. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Locked Up and Criminalized: People on the Move Face a Broken System on Crete’s Shores


Between Delay and Denial 


In the summer of 2025, the government

announced

 the conversion of several military sites, but that announcement was followed by months of silence and effective inaction. Only in February 2026 did the Greek Parliament approve the opening of

two centers

, without specifying their location or how they would be built.


The first details came only months later: in Chania, authorities settled on retrofitting

Agya

, a former exhibition center already in use as a temporary reception facility; in Heraklion, the disused Skouloudis industrial plant was identified instead.


“These delays and constant changes of plan shouldn’t be read as political strategy, but as failure,” Michalis Markodimitrakis, a member of the Heraklion-based collective Thalassa of Solidarity and a researcher at the Hellenic Mediterranean University, told Unicorn Riot.


“Local communities and representatives of Crete’s tourism and cultural sector are pushing back hard, because they see the presence of migrants as damaging to the island’s image and a threat to their economic interests.”


Michalis Markodimitrakis, member of Thalassa of Solidarity collective


A side view of the former Skouloudis industrial facility, where adaptation works to accommodate people on the move have not yet begun. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Back in July 2025, the day after the first announcement floated the opening of the centers, a network of tourism industry associations sent an

open letter

 to Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Migration and …

title: Nouvelles depuis l'inétrieur des CRA lyonnais
content:
Une personne enfermée nous raconte :


Là ils ont sorti la nouvelle loi, ils vont l'appliquer pour tout le monde. [...] Comme A. par exemple, au bout du 90°" jour, à la dernière minute il a eu sa convocation pour le lendemain, il était en train de prendre sa douche et de se préparer pour sortir.

IL

 sort, Îl trouve un policier, convocation pour le lendemain. Ils jouent sur le moral, ils veulent qu'on devienne ouf je sais pas. Il voulait carrément se pendre. Il a mal au cœur.


Selon la nouvelle loi, ce seraient les personnes qui ont été condamnées pour un crime ou délit «

 

passible

 

» de 5 ans d'emprisonnement qui pourraient être enfermées jusqu'à 210 jours.


Pourtant des personnes qui ne rentrent pas dans ces critères voient leur enfermement prolongé. Le procureur avançant la fameuse notion totalement floue de «

 

menace à l'ordre public

 

».


Par l'enfermement toujours plus long et arbitraire en centre de rétention, l'État cherche à détruire psychologiquement les personnes étrangères. Rappelons que les CRAs sont un rouage indispensable au continuum colonial et à la répression raciste subie par celleux enfermé-es.


Franchement, c'est la souffrance ici. On préfère largement la prison qu'ici. [...] Y a la promenade, on sait quel jour on sort. Ici on navigue dans le flou, on sait pas ce qu'il se passe.


 Une autre personne raconte :


Moi je vois un psychologue dehors, je supporte le centre de rétention très difficilement. Moi je suis quelqu'un de complexe, je reste toujours tout seul, mes amis en sont témoins, je peux pas parler avec les gens, j'accepte plus l'enfermement. Même dehors, je suis suivi par un psychiatre, un psychologue, parce que j'ai grandi dans une situation un peu. c'est comme ça… et là on sait pas pourquoi on rentre ici, on est pas dans la guerre

 

? [...]


Ce système il nous dégoûte, c'est pour qu'on rentre.


J'ai peur de parler et qu'on me ramène à l'isolement et qu'ils me frappent. C'est comme ça, c'est la vérité. [...] Mon ami il crie tellement il a mal et ils lui disent “t'as pas mal toi, t'es un menteur”. J'ai honte de te dire ce qu'ils ont dit, par respect, j'ai honte.


Au

CRA

, j'ai vu vraiment le racisme. Dehors, je connais pas. J'ai des amis français, française, je connais pas ça dehors. Juste ici, on dirait des chiens dressés bien, ils rentrent direct, ils te provoquent, ils te cherchent. C'est comme ça, c'est ce que je vois... c'est la vérité. [...] La dernière fois, je suis tombé, tout jaune, les yeux blancs, il a dit “t'as besoin d'un coup de taser, t'es bien toi.”


Ils te font sentir que tu es un danger. Je me sens comme si j'étais un danger pour la France moi.


Y a des gens qui ont pété un câble. Y avait un algérien avec nous, il a pété un câble le pauvre. Le 90

e

 jour, il est sorti et jusqu'à maintenant les gens le cherchent. Sa famille l'a toujours pas trouvé. Toujours on demandait à la police qu'ils lui cherchent un psychiatre, un truc comme ça et ils rigolaient de lui. Chaque jour. Y avait quelqu'un aussi à côté, dans la zone orange. ILa aussi pété un plomb. [...] Il est dans son monde là, il parle n'importe quoi, il sait pas ce qu'il fait, il sait pas où il est.


La parole des personnes enfermées traversent difficilement les murs des CRAs, mais n'oublions pas qu'elles se révoltent. À Lyon, ce mois-ci, des grèves de la faim ont eu lieu et une partie du

CRA

 2 a été incendiée le samedi 5 septembre pour protester contre leurs conditions et l'allongement de leur enfermement.


Organisons-nous, amplifions la lutte pour l'abolition des CRAs, des taules et des frontières

 

!


Soutien et liberté à toutes les personnes enfermées et à leurs proches

title: Shooter of Palestinian College Students Convicted After 3 Years
content:
On Monday, a jury convicted a Vermont man of shooting three Palestinian college students in November 2023.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On Monday, a jury convicted Jason Eaton of attempted murder for shooting three Palestinian college students in November 2023, concluding a case that highlights an increase in anti-Palestinian racism since October 7.

On November 25, 2023, Eaton shot Kinnan Abdalhamid, Tahseen Ali Ahmad, and Hisham Awartani in Burlington, Vermont, after seeing them walk by his apartment. The three students, who were 20 years old at the time, were wearing keffiyehs and speaking in both English and Arabic as they visited the town during the weekend of Thanksgiving.

Eaton walked towards the students and shot them at close range, injuring the three young men and leaving Awartani paralyzed from the waist down.

During the trial, which began on September 14 – nearly three years after the shooting – Eaton’s defense argued that he was legally insane, and that he was suffering from delusions and believed he was instructed to shoot the three students.

But the students and their families have insisted that anti-Palestinian racism was the reason for Eaton’s attack.

In the two months after October 7, 2023, civil rights organizations like the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) documented a “staggering” spike in violence, hate speech, and discrimination against Muslims, Arabs, and Palestinians across the U.S. In one incident, a landlord in Illinois stabbed and killed 6-year-old Palestinian American Wadea Al Fayoume on October 14, one week after October 7.

The prosecution in Eaton’s trial also quoted the shooter using racial slurs, such as that the students had been “dressed up like terrorists” and that they should have been told not to “wear the thing on their head,” referring to their keffiyehs.

The verdict, therefore, is significant for not excusing the shooter’s actions or explaining away his racism.

“The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry,” the families said in a statement, which Awartani’s mother, Elizabeth Price, read after the verdict. “But it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did.”

“During the trial, we had to listen to him use hateful words to describe our sons over and over again. They were not the words of a man confused about who he shot or why. We do not need a jury to tell us why our sons were targeted. We heard it in his own words: this was a hate crime,” Price said.

The Vermont Coalition for Palestinian Liberation, which has organized solidarity with the victims and their families and has sent daily delegations to attend the hearings in support, also issued a statement, calling Eaton’s act “a horrific hate crime.”

“Amidst the racist hysteria the US and Israel whipped up to justify their genocidal war on Gaza, [Eaton] attempted to murder three Palestinian college students,” the statement says.

But the group also pinpoints the movement in solidarity with Palestine as key in transforming consciousness across the country and, in this case, in getting the all-white jury to convict Eaton. This conviction, they write, is in defiance of the “political establishment” and its anti-Palestinian racism, which was on display during the trial.

During the trial, the defense argued that the dozens of supporters in the courthouse must remove their keffiyehs as it would influence the jury – and the judge granted this request.

This is just one example of the struggle over Palestine solidarity, and the state’s anti-Palestinian policies in Vermont. In December 2023, Burlington’s City Council voted down a ceasefire resolution following extensive public testimony in favor, before rejecting a resolution to make Burlington an apartheid-free community multiple times in 2024 and 2026. Burlington has also been the site of the trials of Mohsen Mahdawi and Rümeysa Öztürk, with the local activist community rallying in defense of the Palestine solidarity activists threatened with deportation.

The families of Awartani, Abdalhamid, and Ali Ahmad thanked the local Vermont community for its solidarity in their statement, writing, “That solidarity has mattered even more with each passing year, because our sons’ recovery unfolded alongside the genocide and destruction of Gaza and the escalating ethnic cleansing of the West Bank. While our children fought to heal from …

content:
