title: appel à contribution pour un recueil de fiction anarchiste et anti-autoritaire
content:
cet appel est destiné à n'importe qui partageant des idées anarchistes et anti-autoritaires, que tu écrives des romans ou des nouvelles depuis des annés ou depuis hier, que t'aies jamais rien écrit mais que t'aies plein d'idée et que tes yeux brillent d'envie de les partager, que tu lises tout les jours ou juste un zine de temps en temps.


Qu'est-ce qu'on veut faire ?


on voudrait fabriquer un recueil de textes centré autour de thèmatiques anarchistes et anti-autoritaires. tu peux nous envoyer une nouvelle ultra courte ou très longue, des chansons et même des dessins (mais que en noir et blanc) on aimerait bien avoir une diversité de genre comme de la fantasy, du fantastique, des fan-fiction, de la science-fiction, des récits réalistes ou historiques, des récits qui se passent à notre époque, peu importe. on veut lire des choses tristes, drôles, bizarres ou absurdes, dramatiques ou catarthiques, qui traitent d'impuissance ou de la répression qu'on s'impose, bref des trucs qui font vivre nos idées et/ou résonnent avec notre quotidien politique. on veut créer un objet physique avec tous ces textes. on ne sait pas encore quelle forme ça prendra (revue, livre, zine...) parce qu'on fera en fonction du nombre de contributions qu'on reçoit. on le distribuera uniquement à prix libre (impliquant videmment la gratuité) parce qu'on est contre la marchandisation.


Pourquoi ?


on a envie de proposer ce projet, tout d'abord parce qu'on aime se raconter des histoires entre compas mais aussi parce qu'on aime bien discuter des livres qu'on a lu et d'imaginé comment ça se passerait si les personnages étaient anarchistes. parce qu'on est plein de personnes à avoir des histoires dans nos têtes, ou à griphonner sur des petits carnets et ça donne envie de se partager tout ça. parce qu'on veut ni de la starification des auteurice et des artistes en général ni de leur soit disant exceptionnalité. parce qu'on en a marre de devoir chourrer des livres dans des librairies, livres qui en plus doivent se conformer aux logiques capitalistes et aux normes toutes pourries du monde de l'édition. ça nous fait grave de la curiosité de lire des récit qui ne se plient pas à ces contraintes. parce qu'on veut plus que des imaginaires de conquête, de roi bienveillant ou de technologies sauveuses


parce qu'on veut démarchandiser le fait de partager des histoires par écrit car ême si Internet propose des endroit où il est possible de le faire gratuitement, on refuse de dépendre de réseau sur lesquels on n'a aucun contrôle, qui participent très fortement à l'exploitation de la terre et des humains, ainsi qu'à notre propre surveillance. Alors on lance cet appel parce que potentiellement ça peut créer des rencontres et ça c'est cool.


Thèmes :


 Toustes celleux qui errent ne sont pas perdues.

 La rage est une force qui crée des brèches dans le silence

 Exister au coeur de l'empire


On propose trois phrases qui peuvent t'inspirer. tu en fais ce que tu veux, et si tu t'en éloignes un peu ou complètement on s'en fout. si tu veux les lier ensemble ou en choisir plusieurs ou aucune, c'est super !


Comment ?


on te propose de nous envoyer un texte fan-fiction, fantasy, science fiction, récit historique, auto-fiction, chanson, blague, dessin (noire et blanc)... Ça peut faire deux lignes, 2 pages ou 20. Concernant la manière dont on va choisir les textes, ce sera complètement subjectif. On a aucun critère et on pense pas que notre avis est plus important ou plus éclairé qu'un autre. Dans tous les cas on s'engage a répondre à tous les mails qu'on reçoit. Si t'as envie et que t'en fais la demande explicite, on pourrait se lancer dans un taf « d'édition » comme par exemple des notes sur le texte, proposer des pistes « d'amélioration » ou sur des fautes d'orthographe.Automatic word wrap


On garde en tête que proposer ce genre de travail de réécriture ça peut malgrès nos volontés renforcer des codes et des normes qu'on a envie de détruire.


Peut-importe le format que prendra le recueil, il sera toujours distribué à prix libre sans suggestion de prix et incluant évidemment la gratuité. L'argent ne servira à rémunérer personne, ni auteurice, ni tout autre personne impliquées dans ce projet. On l'utilisera que pour rembourser les frais d'impression et si ce qu'on reçoit est supérieur aux dépenses, ça sera réinvestit dans des projets anti-autoritaires et anarchistes.

author: Unknown
title: «Чёрное знамя»: дело беларусских анархо-партизан во внутренних сводках МВД
content:
Белорусский портал Tribunal.info опубликовал статью об анархистах партизанах из группы «Чёрное знамя».

Неудавшаяся революция 2020 года в Беларуси в медиа-сфере ассоциируется, прежде всего, с яркими и массовыми проявлениями мирного сопротивления. Многотысячные воскресные марши, бело-красно-белые флаги, женские цепи солидарности, дворовые инициативы и демонстративный отказ от насилия сформировали главный визуальный образ беларусской революции.

Однако, события 2020-го не ограничивались только мирными шествиями. Пока большинство противников режима наивно надеялись на мирные перемены, были те, кто, понимая сущность режима, смотрел прагматично. Они решили подойти к разрешению революционного вопроса путём прямого действия.

Речь о четырёх беларусских анархистах - Игоре Олиневиче, Сергее Романове, Дмитрии Резановиче и Дмитрии Дубовском. В прессе и материалах следствия их нередко называют «группой Олиневича» или просто «анархо-партизанами». Сами участники использовали название «Чёрное знамя» — в память об одноимённой анархистской организации, действовавшей на территории Российской империи в начале XX века.

Игорь Олиневич позднее пояснял: «Медиа окрестили нас «группой Олиневича» — или даже «бандой», — но этот ярлык не соответствует действительности. Мы называемся «Чёрное Знамя», в честь одноимённой федерации анархистов, боровшихся на этой земле за свободу ещё в царские времена».

Слева направо: Дмитрий Резанович, Дмитрий Дубовский, Игорь Олиневич, Сергей Романов

Игорь Олиневич — вчера ему исполнилось 43 года. Один из наиболее известных представителей беларусского анархистского движения. Получил техническое образование, в 2000-е годы включился в деятельность анархистских инициатив. Широкую известность приобрел после уголовного дела, связанного с серией акций прямого действия против государственных и коммерческих объектов.

В ноябре 2010 года его фактически похитили в Москве, после чего он оказался в застенках спецслужб РБ. В 2011 году Олиневича приговорили к восьми годам лишения свободы. Правозащитные организации признали его политическим заключённым. В 2015 году он вышел на свободу в результате т.н. «политической оттепели» и покинул Беларусь.

В заключении Игорь написал книгу «Еду в Магадан», основанную на тюремном опыте, в последствии изданную на многих языках мира. Осенью 2020 года он вновь оказался в Беларуси и, согласно материалам дела, стал одним из участников подпольной группы.

Дмитрий Дубовский родился в 1986 году в Солигорске. В анархистском движении с конца 2000-х годов. После возбуждения уголовных дел против беларусских анархистов в 2010 году покинул страну. На протяжении почти десяти лет находился в бегах, в том числе жил в России и Украине. Много путешествовал, о чем даже писал заметки, публиковавшиеся на сайте анархо-группы «Революционное действие».

Его имя фигурировало в материалах старых уголовных дел, связанных с нападениями на государственные и коммерческие объекты. После задержания в 2020 году эти эпизоды вновь стали предметом расследования.

Сергей Романов родился в 1994 году в Гомеле. Он самый молодой участник группы. К моменту событий 2020 года он уже имел опыт столкновения с правоохранительной системой режима. Ранее его судили по делу о незаконном обороте оружия. После освобождения оставался под превентивным надзором милиции. В материалах нового дела это обстоятельство использовалось как подтверждение того, что правоохранительные органы считали его подготовленным к подпольной деятельности и обращению с оружием.

В заключении Сергей проявил себя, как художник. Он активно создавал из подручных материалов зарисовки, которые передавались на волю. В частности, в рамках арт-проекта художника Владислава Бохана, с творчеством Сергея Романова смогли познакомиться зрители в Польше, Германии и Италии. Вероятно, из-за этого тюремная цензура перестала пропускать его работы.

Дмитрий Резанович родился в 1989 году. Связан с беларусским анархистским движением задолго до 2020 года. В сравнении с Олиневичем и Дубовским он значительно реже упоминается в СМИ. Тем не менее, следствие рассматривало Резановича, как полноправного участника группы, принимавшего участие в подготовке и проведении акций прямого действия. В ночь с 28 на 29 октября 2020 года его задержали вместе с Олиневичем, Романовым и Дубовским неподалёку от беларусско-украинской границы.

История «Чёрного знамени» уже неоднократно пересказывалась СМИ, заявлениях правозащитников, материалах суда и письмах самих заключённых. Однако, в этой статье мы ещё раз …

author: Unknown
title: La bombe n'est pas à nous : pourquoi les anarchistes reparlent de l'arme nucléaire
content:
Lyon, le 22 septembre. Alors que les États augmentent leurs budgets militaires et modernisent leurs arsenaux nucléaires, les services sociaux ferment et les militant·es sont poursuivi·es. Les groupes anarchistes et antimilitaristes lyonnais appellent à relier la lutte contre l'arme nucléaire aux conflits sociaux du quotidien — et à descendre dans la rue pour une marche contre l'arme nucléaire à la fin du mois.


Ce qui se passe


Les dépenses mondiales consacrées aux programmes nucléaires continuent d'augmenter, malgré les déclarations sur le désarmement. La France, qui fait partie des puissances nucléaires, conserve et modernise son arsenal — tout en réduisant le financement des hôpitaux, des écoles et du logement social. Les sites militaires restent des zones de secret et de répression : les manifestations y sont interdites, les militant·es poursuivi·es, l'information verrouillée.


Pourquoi ça nous concerne


Pour les anarchistes, l'arme nucléaire n'est pas une menace abstraite : c'est la forme ultime du pouvoir étatique. La décision de vie ou de mort de millions de personnes est prise par une poignée d'individus, tandis que les conséquences pèsent sur tout le monde. Chaque euro investi dans des ogives est un euro volé aux hôpitaux, aux écoles et au logement. La logique qui sous-tend l'arsenal nucléaire est la même que celle qui sous-tend le déblocage des camps, l'expulsion des squats et l'interdiction des grèves.


Nous ne pouvons pas «

 

faire sauter

 

» les arsenaux seuls. Mais nous pouvons dénoncer le militarisme, relier la lutte pour le logement et le climat à la critique de la machine de guerre, soutenir les initiatives antinucléaires — et construire des structures horizontales plutôt que des verticales de la peur.


Ce que nous pouvons faire


Venir aux actions antinucléaires et antiguerre — marches, piquets, blocages.


Soutenir les grèves et les mouvements sociaux — relier le militarisme à l'exploitation quotidienne.


Exiger la transparence des budgets militaires et dénoncer la propagande de la «

 

sécurité

 

».


Construire l'entraide et des réseaux de solidarité locaux.


📢 Marche contre l'arme nucléaire — Lyon


Samedi 17 octobre, 14h00


Rassemblement : Place Bellecour, Lyon


Itinéraire : Bellecour → Préfecture → Base aérienne 942 (Mont Verdun)


Nous ne descendons pas seulement contre la bombe. Nous descendons contre l'État qui dépense pour la guerre ce qui nous est volé. Contre le militarisme qui tue ici et maintenant — à Gaza, en Ukraine, au Soudan et dans nos rues. Contre le pouvoir qui décide à notre place si nous vivons ou non.


Revendications de la marche :


Réduction des dépenses militaires et réorientation des moyens vers les services sociaux.


Fermeture des sites nucléaires et des bases militaires sur le territoire.


Liberté de manifester et fin des poursuites contre les antimilitaristes.


Non à la guerre — ici comme partout.


Apportez : banderoles, pancartes, instruments de musique, de l'eau, de la solidarité. Bloc de solidarité avec les grèves sociales — rassemblement à 13h30 à Place Guichard (près de la sortie du métro, Lyon 3

e

).


Toutes les annonces, la logistique et le contact — sur Telegram : t.me/Stop_Bombe_Lyon


La bombe n'est pas à nous. Elle appartient au pouvoir qui ne nous a pas consulté·es. Venez — et montrez que la décision doit être la nôtre, pas la leur.


Note sur le lieu : la Base aérienne 942 (Mont Verdun) est un site militaire réel de la région lyonnaise, situé au nord de Lyon (Monts d'Or). Elle abrite un centre de commandement souterrain et joue un rôle dans la défense aérienne et la dissuasion. Elle a déjà été la cible d'actions directes de militant·es antinucléaires dans les années 1970, ce qui rend ce point d'arrivée symboliquement et historiquement cohérent.

content:

1. Anarchy, acracy and the rule of the archons


by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here


Because the term “anarchy” is so often used pejoratively to mean chaos, and because some contemporary anarchists are 

far from freedom-loving

, [1] people often look for a less off-putting term to describe the future society they would like to see.


I personally took to using “

real anarchism

” [2] to mark my own position, while others call themselves “voluntaryists” and here in France “

libertaires

“.


One term that is sometimes used to replace “anarchy” is “acracy”, although I suspect the label “acracist” is a non-starter for obvious reasons!


“Anarchy” 

means

 the absence of any “archy”, any form of government or rule, such as monarchy or oligarchy, [3] while “acracy” 

means

 the absence of any “cracy”, which is to say any coercive authority, such as plutocracy or so-called democracy. [4]


The term 

acracia

 first appeared in the Iberian world and is 

believed

 to have been invented by the Catalan syndicalist Rafael Farga i Pellicer (1844-1890), who founded a journal with that name. [5]


It was used by the likes of 

Peter Kropotkin

 (1842-1921) [6] and 

Martin Buber

 (1878-1965) [7] as a synonym for anarchy, but is seen by some as conveying the idea of a society that is 

ordered

, albeit in a voluntary and consensual manner, and/or as one without any kind of 

exploitation

 rather than without any kind of 

authority

, as is the case with anarchy. [8]


In a 2018 

interview

, French economist and thinker Frédéric Lordon argued that, etymologically, anarchy means the absence of an absolute foundation (

ᾰ̓ρχή, ărkhḗ

) on which power’s commandments can be based.


He said that because its political meaning is, in fact, a society in which there is neither power nor domination, the word should really be replaced by acracy, which is precisely that absence of power and domination (

κρατία, kratía

). [9]


With due respect to Lordon, the question does not seem to be as clear as he suggests. While the root word 

krátos

 can indeed 

mean

 “power, might”, [10] it can also mean an “act of strength, act of valour”, with the postulated Proto-Indo-European stem 

kret

 

also

 indicating “intelligence”. [11]


So acracy could alternatively be interpreted as a society without strength, valour and intelligence.


I think we may already be there!


Meanwhile, the 

ărkhḗ

 opposed by anarchy can be 

traced back

 to the verb 

ắrkhō

 which means, in the transitive sense, “to lead; to rule; to govern; to command” and, in the intransitive sense, “to be ruler; to hold an archonship”. [12]


My ears pricked up at that last word!


Historically, an archon 

was

 a chief magistrate of ancient Athens and more generally “a person who claims the right to rule, or to exercise power or sovereign authority over other human beings” or simply “a ruler, head of state or other leader”. [13]


But in the gnostic tradition it identifies “a supernatural ruler of the cosmos”. William Thompson has 

described

 “the cry of the archon Ialdabaoth that he was the Lord of the Universe and that there was nothing beyond him”. [14]


Per Shapiro writes about the archons in his book 

The War on Life: How We Are Manipulated by Archontic Intelligence

, which I 

reviewed

 in May this year. [15]


He explains that the archontic influence in our world is a psychopathic one which refuses to respect natural boundaries and human taboos: “In this range, we find everything from incest, rape and perversions to various manifestations of hubris, such as genetically manipulated crops, laboratory-made life and the fission of the atomic nucleus”. [16]


He sees this phenomenon as taking its most extreme form with Yahweh, the god of the Old Testament, who for the gnostics was a pretender god, “an insane demon who has the delusion of having created the universe. A deranged being who is jealous of the living planet and wants to destroy it”. [17]


There is definitely an anarchic flavour to the message from Sophia (Mother Earth) to archon leader Ialdabaoth: “The authority you claim rests on deception, and when the deception fails, you perish”. [18]


Per quotes author John Lamb Lash as saying …

A few days ago, Sudan’s political and military authorities came together and presented a proposal for what they call a “Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue,” aimed at reaching the broadest possible front to form a government in partnership with the military forces. This is something the military and Islamists in Sudan take pride in, but it is not a new step in the political reality. It is a recycled tactic that was previously used under Bashir’s regime through what was called the “National Dialogue.” The forces involved in that process were largely those allied with the military regime, while the revolutionary opposition did not make a significant difference.

Today, a politically oriented committee is being formed with a new propaganda framework. We see figures who once criticized the policies of the authorities, such as Dr. Mohamed Jalal Hashim, Al-Badri, and other intellectuals associated with the authorities, submitting to Al-Burhan’s policy, which aims to legitimize military rule. With the clear popular and imperial rejection of the Muslim Brotherhood as an active organization in Sudan, the army has sought to use forces that were previously considered part of the revolution to legitimize and institutionalize its upcoming policies.

The army’s position became clear in the statement by its Chief of Staff, Yasser Abdel Rahman Al-Atta, regarding Al-Burhan potentially running for four terms, equivalent to 20 years in power. At the same time, intellectuals close to the authorities are attempting to legitimize the old political system, while imperialist forces are trying to exploit revolutionary positions in accordance with their own agendas.

This leaves many revolutionaries uncertain about what political tactics can preserve the continuity of the revolution and complete its objectives: overthrowing the authoritarian regime and carrying out a social revolution.

The war was a means for the Islamists to return to power after the overwhelming popular rejection they had faced. Their systematic policies of revenge were clear, including in their own speeches, and this is widely acknowledged. But let us look at where they have reached today.

If the Sudanese people, during the December Revolution, rejected the Islamist regime by around 50 percent, then today that rejection may be closer to 80 percent, for several reasons.

Islamist organizations have constructed a political equation that depends on violence to maintain popular support—not only violence carried out by them, but also violence carried out by the Rapid Support Forces. author: Julius Gavroche
title: The political topography of anarchism
content:
Olaus Magnus, detail from

Carta Marina

, 1539


On old maps, it is common to see areas populated by mythological creatures, mermaids and Amazons, dragons and unicorns. The beings that inhabit the most remote and unexplored regions – those known or presumed to exist, but which are not yet understood – are depicted in great detail. The accounts of the few travellers who have reached these places are passed on by word of mouth and become distorted as they are retold; they are magnified and exaggerated, until from a narrative—presumed to be more or less reliable—an entire imaginary topography emerges, which serves at the same time to prove the existence of the mythical creatures whose territory it delineates. The circular reasoning is evident.  Dragons exist because they live there, at the edge of the world. This places them on the map. And they live there because they exist and must be somewhere. That is why they can feature in the depiction of the world.


Similarly, in the nineteenth century, with the fantastical excesses of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance now a thing of the past, Victorian explorers – salacot hats on their heads and rifles at the ready – set about methodically filling in the gaps that still remained on the maps. Particularly on the African continent, these blank spaces acted as magnets for the colonial powers, which meticulously mapped out the coastline, yet still knew nothing of what lay inland. This presented a seemingly irresistible invitation to minds imbued with evangelising and imperialist fantasies. After all, as Kipling reminds us, it is the white man’s burden. Something similar occurs in politics too. Most of us grow up virtually as functionally illiterate in this sphere, which is not normally considered necessary for adult education. Generally speaking, the education system and society as a whole take the view that a country’s inhabitants must acquire a body of knowledge that will equip them as future workers and productive members of society, but this does not extend to the civic skills essential for political engagement.


Be that as it may, the fact remains that current democratic models restrict effective participation to a caste of professionals, which means that the rest of the population need only possess a bare inkling of how the system works – just enough to cast a vote in a ballot box and accept that the direct management of their affairs is no longer, if you’ll pardon the redundancy, their concern. But it seems that the tendency to invent what one does not know is a constant feature of human psychology. Just like the monsters on medieval maps, the political landscape is riddled with dark and unknown zones – grey areas of which one usually has only vague notions – from which a fantastical image is constructed that replaces more detailed knowledge and makes the latter seem unnecessary. On the basis of these vague notions, the political landscape is divided up, associating certain elements of the ideological spectrum with distant cardinal points and populating it with the corresponding mythological creatures that inhabit it. Evidently, these beings are not a spontaneous product of the imagination, but are often supplied by interested parties, through channels suited to the level of representation being sought. Cinema, television and, above all, the mainstream media supplant formal political education (in the broadest sense), and disseminate prejudices and preconceived images across a mental map that is intuited rather than drawn. Thus, most people (though not all) know that National Socialism lies somewhere to the right (the east?) of the conservatives, but not exactly why, or what the differences between them are. Similarly, the Marxist left lies to the west, in a zone populated by enemies of private property, although nobody knows how they got there, or why. And the anarchists? That’s where the dragons are…


If our knowledge of, shall we say, conventional political options is generally sketchy and vague, our understanding of those that transcend the conventions of the civic common sense of an era enters the realm of the nebulous. We find ourselves on fertile ground for the mythical. Any notion that goes beyond the parameters accepted as unquestionable in the foundations of the current democratic system is perceived as nonsense, difficult to take on board or even to conceive of as possible. Everyone knows that someone has to be in charge, and if not, things descend into …

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa
content:
History in the Horn of Africa is rarely allowed to remain history. An ancient civilization becomes evidence of modern sovereignty. A medieval dynasty becomes proof of national continuity. Territory incorporated during one political era is later remembered as though it had always belonged to the state that governed it.


This habit has become especially visible as the Red Sea has returned to Ethiopian political discourse. Ethiopia is landlocked and has obvious economic reasons to seek dependable maritime trade. But there is a fundamental difference between negotiating the use of a port and claiming that a neighboring country possesses territory that properly belongs to Ethiopia. That distinction disappears when Assab is described as a “lost Ethiopian port.”


Ethiopia did not lose a sovereign port in 1993. Eritrea recovered sovereignty over territory that had been incorporated into Ethiopia after the violation and eventual termination of an internationally established federal arrangement. To describe this as Ethiopia “losing the sea” begins the story at the moment of Ethiopian possession and ignores how that possession came about.


This is what I mean by imperial nostalgia.


Imperial nostalgia is not merely admiration for emperors or attachment to an earlier age. It is a way of remembering political space. Territory once incorporated into an empire is remembered not simply as territory once governed, but as territory that naturally belonged there. Incorporation becomes ownership, ownership becomes entitlement, and independence can then be remembered as national loss.


Christopher Clapham’s notion of an Ethiopian “manifest destiny” is useful at the margins of this argument, although I invoke him cautiously and not to validate Ethiopian historical claims. The phrase captures a mentality in which expansion can stop looking like expansion when incorporation is presented as the fulfillment of history. Manifest destiny looks forward. Imperial nostalgia looks backward and imagines that a geography produced through expansion was the natural order all along.


The deeper problem is the projection of modern states backward into political worlds that did not organize themselves according to contemporary borders. Aksum is an obvious example. Its political and commercial world crossed territories that are now divided between Eritrea and Ethiopia and formed part of a much larger Red Sea system.

UNESCO’s account of Aksum

 describes an ancient civilization. It does not describe a modern territorial state possessing a contemporary claim to the Red Sea.


Calling Aksum simply “ancient Ethiopia” imports the political geography of today into antiquity. Calling it “ancient Eritrea” would make the same mistake. Civilizations, languages, religions, trading networks, and archaeological landscapes regularly cross the boundaries of modern states. Shared history does not create shared sovereignty.


I explored this problem more fully in

There Is No Timeless Eritrea or Ethiopia

. The point is not to diminish the history of either country. It is to stop asking ancient civilizations to perform the work of modern territorial law. Aksum should be studied as Aksum rather than recruited into a contemporary argument over Assab.


Richard Reid examined this problem directly in

The Trans-Mereb Experience: Perceptions of the Historical Relationship between Eritrea and Ethiopia

. Reid is useful because he is skeptical of efforts on either side to recruit antiquity into modern nationalism. The same history can be arranged to prove a supposedly eternal Ethiopia or, in the opposite direction, an Eritrea with no meaningful historical relationship to communities south of the Mereb. Neither approach is good history.


Even the word Ethiopia should make us cautious. The Greek term

Aithiopia

 did not refer neatly to the bounded territorial state called Ethiopia today. Recognizing this does not make modern Ethiopia less legitimate. It simply acknowledges that political names, communities, and territorial states change over time.


Eritrea should be approached in exactly the same way. Fred Halliday, writing in 1971 while the Eritrean war was still underway, acknowledged in

“The Fighting in Eritrea”

 that Eritrea in its modern territorial form had been defined under European colonialism. That fact does not weaken Eritrean sovereignty. It places Eritrea within the history of modern Africa.


Most African states inherited territorial forms created or …

author: M.P
title: Abya Yala aborta y descoloniza
content:
Descolonizar el aborto es romper con la idea de que el conocimiento se produce lejos de la vida. Nuestros pueblos han abortado, cuidado, acompañado, sanado y compartido saberes mucho antes de que la academia o las instituciones necesitaran llamarlos evidencia para reconocerlos.

Esos conocimientos no existen separados de quienes los sostienen. Viven en la memoria colectiva, en la palabra compartida, en los pueblos originarios, en las comunidades negras, en los barrios, las periferias y las redes que sostienen la vida. No son materia prima para extraer, traducir y convertir en autoridad lejos de quienes los construyen.

Descolonizar el aborto no significa reemplazar una verdad por otra. Significa romper con la pretensión de que una sola verdad pueda nombrarnos a todas. Defender muchas formas de conocer, abortar, cuidar y acompañar sin imponerles una única manera de existir.

Este Día de Acción Global exigimos aborto libre para América Latina, sin borrar las historias, los saberes y los pueblos que lo han hecho posible.

Porque nunca hubo una sola historia del aborto. Que nadie vuelva a contar la nuestra como si no hubiéramos estado ahí.

#28S#AbortoLibre#DescolonizaElAborto

author: Nada Elia
title: Women and Youth Are at the Forefront of the Struggle for Palestinian Liberation
content:
They follow in the footsteps of Palestinian women and children who have resisted colonialism in the past century.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

I grew up in a household of women and children that, as my sisters and I matured, eventually became a household of only women. My father was frequently gone on long overseas business trips before his untimely death when I was seven. I often wonder if this is the reason the expression “women and children” strikes me as essentially flawed: It suggests that women and children are the more vulnerable members of society, rather than its resilient survivors. It infantilizes women by grouping them with children, rather than adult men.

In the context of a national struggle, it strips women of agency, as if such agency can only manifest through armed revolt. In a military context, the expression “women and children” — or “womenandchildren,” to use the term coined by antimilitary feminist scholar Cynthia Enloe — presumes that women and children never take up arms or participate in resistance, even as we see such actions occurring in numerous struggles around the world. And in listing casualties, it implies that men’s deaths and injuries are less tragic, less mournable.

In the case of Palestine, women and youth have led, and continue to lead, some of the most transformative efforts and initiatives in our people’s quest for justice — that is, our resistance first to imperialism, then to settler colonialism and apartheid. They have not been spared Israel’s violence, just for being women, or children, and many have been and remain at the forefront of popular resistance to Zionism’s ultimate aim of eliminating all Palestinians. While this may have become more obvious during Israel’s accelerated genocidal assault on Gaza following Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks, it had always been clear to anyone not deliberately looking away.

From a number of uprisings over the past century in Palestine, it is obvious that youth, “the children,” are not just among the leaders; they are the more effective, more transformational leaders. Unfettered by traditions and social norms they do not relate to, they engage in novel forms of organizing, seeking the complete abolition of oppressive systems, rather than their reversal. And women, in their capacity as autonomous adults, rather than merely as wives and mothers, have consistently resisted both the imperial ideology targeting their country, and the military assaults that accompanied it. They did so while providing men, as well as the youth and children, the moral, emotional, and practical support the Palestinian people need in order to persist. This was perhaps most evident on a global scale during the 1987–93 Intifada, when women organized most of the popular committees tending to the educational, nutritional, and health needs of Palestinians resisting Israel’s clampdown, as youth took to the streets daily to express their rejection of Israel’s decades-long oppressive rule. These defenseless children hurled rocks at armored tanks, fully aware of the hefty price they would pay for their defiant act, because they knew that risking limb and life is preferable to living without freedom and dignity.

Women’s and children’s agency is enacted daily in the courage of girls such as Janna Jihad, who was dubbed “the world’s youngest journalist” when she started documenting Israel’s crimes at a mere seven years of age. Jihad started recording Israel’s attacks using her mother’s cell phone, posting her recordings far and wide on social media. She has repeatedly said that her camera is her weapon of choice. Jihad is the cousin of Ahed Tamimi, the “lioness” who has confronted heavily armed Israeli soldiers determined to take over her village lands since she was a toddler. Israel imprisoned Tamimi for eight months when she was sixteen; she used the time behind bars to read up on international law, later enrolling in college planning to go to law school, so as to hold Israel accountable for its violations. “I am a freedom fighter. So I will not be the victim,” she told journalists upon her release.

Palestinian children’s agency was also clear in the 2022 uprising of rebellious youth standing up to Israel’s might. Ibrahim al-Nabulsi, dubbed “the Lion of Nablus,” was eighteen when he was brutally assassinated by the Israeli Occupation Forces. Following his martyrdom, his mother, Huda al-Nabulsi …

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 


Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt.

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       


In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.


An anthropological base map of Plateau Province reproduced from C.G. Ames, The Gazetteers of Plateau Province, 1932 (Copy in Nigerian National Archives, Kaduna)


The highlands were ideal for the crop. Potatos thrive in cooler conditions, and Jos and Mambila provided the climate colonial agronomists desired. However, these areas were not empty spaces waiting for improvement. They were inhabited, farmed, and politically complex societies with their own crops, markets, and knowledge systems.


Colonial rule altered the dynamics in these regions. Tin mining on the Jos Plateau attracted workers, administrators, and settlers. Demand for European foods increased. Potatos, once a garden crop for expatriates and mission stations, began to seem valuable to the colonial state.


Starting in the 1930s, British

officials based in Nigeria began importing seed potatos from Ireland, Britain, Europe, South Africa, the Canary Islands, and the United States.

 Mission stations cultivated the potatos. District heads distributed the seed. Farmers cautiously tried the crop, incorporating it into local routines where it made sense while rejecting it when it didn’t. The potato became a means of power.


This did not mean that older crops and seed systems disappeared. There was no formal ban, and local farmers continued to grow, save, and exchange seed in various ways. The scheme worked in subtler ways: it altered the rewards. Access to land, labour, credit, official support, and markets began to favour the colonial crop. Imported seed was seen as improved, while farmer-saved seed and local knowledge were pushed to the sidelines. Over time, diverse and adaptable seed systems were narrowed, though not completely erased, by a supply chain prioritising mines, mission stations, military demands, and imperial markets.


Before the Second World War, the scheme was no great success. Some farmers thought potatos were poisonous. Others saw no reason to cultivate a crop with a limited, European-dominated market. A 1937 attempt to sell imported ‘Great Scott’ seed potatos to the Jos Native Authority ended poorly: half went unsold, the remainder was given away, and the scheme lost money.


War transformed failure into urgency. The empire needed food close to military outposts. It aimed to save cargo space and lessen reliance on disrupted shipping routes. Suddenly, potatos on the Mambila and Jos Plateau became crucial.


The war economy and the creation of dependency


Production surged from around

90 tons at the beginning of the war in 1939 to about 1,200 tons by 1943. Seed stores and experimental stations emerged throughout Kagoro, Zonkwa, Kurmin Biri, and Riyom

. Colonial science advanced rapidly, too: London-based Kew scientists devised ways to transport sprouting ‘eyes’ of potatos instead of whole tubers, facilitating a steady supply from outside.


Wartime officials did not establish an independent Nigerian seed system; they created a supply chain. Farmers were encouraged to boost production. Yet, this authority remained elsewhere: seed, disease control, imports, and markets remained …

author: Ngozi Nwosu-Juba
title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?
content:
During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.” This was widely regarded as progressive, even transformative, evidence that we had moved beyond paternalistic approaches and were empowering women to speak for themselves. It became a powerful narrative, one that resonated strongly with donors and development agencies alike.

Yet, over time, this language began to lose its appeal, as I started to interrogate the assumptions that underpinned it. Were women truly without voices, or were their voices simply being ignored, dismissed, or rendered unintelligible within systems of power?

The notion of “giving voice” positioned organizations like ours as benevolent intermediaries bestowing agency on those presumed to lack it. In doing so, it risked obscuring the fact that women had always spoken, resisted, negotiated, and articulated their realities, often in ways that did not fit donor expectations or development frameworks.

What does it mean to “give” women a voice? And who has the authority to bestow something that women have always possessed?

There is a long history of women’s resistance and political agency in Africa. In Nigeria, the

Women’s War of 1929

 stands as a powerful reminder that women have never been silent. Thousands of women in eastern Nigeria organized, mobilized, challenged colonial authority, and articulated their demands with remarkable courage and clarity. Their actions were neither facilitated by development projects nor enabled by donor-funded interventions. They emerged from women’s own collective consciousness, an inherited legacy of women’s determination to resist injustice.

In the Bamenda Grassfields of Northwest Cameroon, women organized one of the most significant grassroots uprisings against colonial authority in Central and West Africa. Faced with colonial policies that threatened their farmland, the women of Kom fought back.

Using

Anlu

, a traditional practice where women collectively sanction men who violate community norms, they organized marches and used satire to name and shame colonial collaborators. Through their actions, they brought administrative and economic life in the region to a standstill for months, and their protest ultimately forced the colonial government to reverse the land policies and contributed to the broader political shifts that shaped Cameroon’s path toward independence and reunification.

In Eastern Africa, Queen Muhumuza led a movement against British and German colonialists from Southern Uganda. According to the historian

Murindwa Rutanga

, Queen Muhumuza was the first major leader to mobilize peasants in Kigezi into organized anticolonial resistance against British rule starting in 1909. Drawing on her political experience and spiritual authority, she raised consciousness about the dangers of colonialism and united a broad sector of the Bakiga and neighboring communities in armed resistance. Under her leadership, communities resisted colonial boundary demarcations, obstructed missionaries and colonial agents, and challenged the expansion of colonial authority despite violent repression. Her efforts established her as one of the …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

“Revolutionary Cuba wrote the rulebook on resilience,” Yaffe said. Facing a total oil blockade since January, Cuba is now undertaking an incredibly rapid transition to renewable energies.

“Many commentators are saying this will be the fastest ever transition.” Solar panel parks now supply more than 60% of electricity on some days, but Yaffe said the challenge is storage.

Singaporean ecosocialist See Yong Feng, another guest speaker, told Green Left that capitalism is holding back human development.

“The need for limitless economic growth is often framed as the only way to solve global poverty, but new research strongly disproves this. The world already uses way more than enough energy and materials to provide a decent standard of living for all, but the profit-driven capitalist system prevents this from happening.

“We can both address poverty and the climate crisis, as long as we break the capitalist elites’ control of our economy and democratise our production and consumption,” See said.

The Gaza genocide, Trump’s blatant disregard for international and domestic laws and his naked colonial violence symbolise the ugly reality that is forging a new generation of activists, Alex Bainbridge, a conference organiser, told GL.

“Trump has his admirers and imitators all around the world, including Marine Le Pen in France, Narendra Modi in India and Pauline Hanson here.

“But while far-right politicians push hard, there is a sharp reaction and a growing resistance; this conference was a powerful reminder of that,” Bainbridge said.

Remah Naji, a leading activist with Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, expressed this resistance. “Maybe we can’t stop a fascist and psychopath like Netanyahu from committing the war crimes he’s committing … but I can hold my government to account.”

The conference included a solidarity concert with Phil Monsour and an art exhibition.

Markela Panegyres, another conference organiser and curator of the art exhibition, told GL: “From the ongoing genocide in Gaza, to the endless drive to more wars and militarism, to ecocide, to the rise of the far right, the depravity of US-led imperialism and global capitalism is reaching ever-higher levels.

“The gravity of this moment demands that art and artists play an active role in resistance.

“This is why the concept of cultural intifada is so important: Art should not be merely a reflection of life, or entertainment or a commodity, but a weapon in the struggle for our collective liberation.

“The work of the artists, musicians and theatre makers who participated in the cultural intifada round-table and exhibition demonstrated the importance of art in movement-building.

“We were so proud that Aunty Sue Coleman-Haseldine, a senior Googatha Elder, Maralinga survivor and long-term anti-nuclear activist, came all the way from the Googatha Nation in the west of South Australia, north of Ceduna.”

Coleman-Haseldine talked about the campaign against rocket and weapons testing on her Country and her opposition to AUKUS and to US military and surveillance bases.

Ecosocialism 2026 was sponsored by the Socialist Alliance, Green Left, Resistance Books and Links — International …

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The Historiographical Legacy of B.A. Ogot and His Generation
content:
Good evening, colleagues, and the Governor of Kisumu County, Professor Anyang Nyong’o! It is truly a pleasure for me to join you in this commemoration of the towering historian, scholar, and public intellectual, Bethwell Alan Ogot. I believe I speak on behalf of all of us in extending our deep gratitude to the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA) and the Department of History at Kenyatta University for organizing this important conference. Personally, my appreciation extends to that rarity of experiences, the opportunity to meet several of my former students at Kenyatta University between 1984 and 1989 who have become distinguished academics and administrators. It’s a befitting tribute to our intellectual father, grandfather, quickly becoming a great-grandfather, who was raised and spent his last years and is buried in nearby Yala, that this conference is being held in his home city of Kisumu, under the transformative leadership of one of Kenya’s leading scholars and public intellectuals, Governor Peter Anyang Nyong’o.


Introduction


Let me begin by noting that I last visited Kisumu in January 2019 to join Professor Ogot as he celebrated his 90th birthday. I first visited this city nearly forty years earlier, in 1980, when I was doing research for my doctoral dissertation on Kenyan economic and labor history, and spent time at this venue, the Tom Mboya Labor College. Professor Ogot had a lot to do with my interest in Kenyan history. My engagement with him goes back to 1976 when he served as external examiner at the University of Malawi.


Years later, he would proudly tell audiences at events where both of us were present that I owed my degree with distinction to him! In our classes on East African history, we had read Ogot’s books, and it was an indescribable honor and privilege to meet him in person. I was deeply touched and humbled when he asked to meet the student who had received the distinction, and he prevailed upon the department to bring me to the cottage along Lake Malawi, where the department took him to show their gratitude for bestowing the department with the distinction of his presence. .


That was the beginning of a lifelong mentoring and intellectual relationship that changed the trajectory of my personal and professional life, on which I will say more later.


When Professor Ogot passed away in January 2025, there was an avalanche of tributes in the popular and academic media celebrating his life and immense scholarly contributions. It is befitting that we are gathered here to remember and celebrate him as a towering historian and intellectual polymath.


Ogot belongs to an exceptional generation of the pioneering architects of the African academy in its multifaceted epistemic and institutional dimensions. These were extraordinary individuals, inspired by the fierce historical and humanistic urgency and imperatives of African nationalism: decolonization, nation-building, regional integration, development, and democracy. They were driven by the audacity, passion, and commitment to remaking the production, dissemination, and consumption of knowledge in, and for, Africa and the world.


They were scholar-activists who transformed existing disciplines and founded new ones, who built interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary paradigms, perspectives and practices, who believed in the power of education as a public good and engine of development, who relished their role as rigorous academics and public intellectuals, who jealously guarded academic freedom and the intelligentsia as the conscience of their new nation-states.


Their lives were large, complex, and multilayered. The trajectory of Ogot’s career is quite emblematic of his peers, born between the third and fourth decades of the twentieth century in the immediate aftermath of the formation of the colonial conquest state, whose ideologues deluded themselves would last for centuries, if not millennia, only to collapse spectacularly as Ogot and his peers matured into adulthood. I would like to explore, rather briefly given the limitations of time, five aspects of Professor Ogot’s remarkable life and legacy: Ogot the man, the historian, the institution builder, the public figure, and the mentor. Let me add that today we’ve heard much about many of these themes. My excuse for revisiting them is that I came a long way, and I have to justify my ticket!


Ogot the Man

Le 24 septembre 1853, un colon Français pose le pied à Balade, un village sur une île du Pacifique Sud, la Kanaky. Il prend possession de l'île au nom de la France. Cette date symbolise aujourd'hui le jour de la prise de possession et le début du colonialisme en Kanaky.


Depuis 1853, les

kanak

De 1888 à 1946, ils furent confinés dans des réserves et régis par le Code de l'indigénat qui les maintenait en dehors du droit commun.


Les Kanak ont toujours manifesté leur opposition à cette colonisation, mais les incessants soulèvements furent tous réprimés brutalement par l'administration française.


Parmi les plus mémorables résistances, il y a le soulèvement de 1878 conduits par Ataï et d'autres chefs kanak visant la prise de la capitale, Nouméa,

“For too long, Israel’s policies in the West Bank have been treated or looked at as isolated events,” says Ori Givati, director of international relations at B’Tselem. “We actually find that there is one very coherent logic behind all of them, and this is the logic of elimination of Palestinian collective life in the West Bank.” Givati says tactics against Palestinians intensified with Israel’s 2022 election and again after October 7, 2023, adding that “we are definitely seeing a lot of the mechanisms, the tools that were used and are used still … in Gaza, being implemented in the West Bank.”

We also speak with Mohammad Sha’ban, a Palestinian farmer from Halhul in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank who says 11 gates and seven settler outposts have been installed around Halhul since 2025. “We cannot reach our lands. We cannot go outside Halhul. They open only one gate from 8 o’clock until 5 o’clock every day,” says Sha’ban. author: Ruby Healer
title: Labor doubles down on US military alliance
content:
“American force posture in Australia is growing”, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles declared on his visit to Washington, DC, this month. “Since we’ve come to government”, Marles said, standing alongside US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, “you can see a through line there of growing American force posture in Australia”.

It was a fairly straightforward summary of the Albanese Labor government’s attitude, followed up with promises of further integration between the Australian and US militaries. A shifting “force posture” will mean more American troop rotations, more US air and naval operations and more pre-positioning of military equipment like warplanes, fuel and munitions in Australia.

Agreements made by the Albanese government will ramp up co-operation on all fronts, with a newly

revitalised

 HMAS Stirling base near Perth set to host American nuclear-powered submarines and an estimated 2,300 US troops within five years. As America’s military machine looks ahead to an era of aggressive contest with China in the Asia-Pacific, Australia’s ruling class is desperate to make itself an indispensable part of US war planning.

Weapons trade regulations have also been

loosened

 under a bilateral agreement to help both countries access shared research to develop arms and surveillance systems. And, Marles promised ominously, “you will hear more from us ... in the coming months” about further arrangements to increase co-operation.

Of course, there’s nothing new about the Australian ruling class throwing itself into a military alliance with the United States. This is a long-standing arrangement pursued by every Australian government since the Second World War. Permanent joint intelligence and communications programs have run out of Pine Gap in the Northern Territory and the Harold Holt naval station in Western Australia since the 1960s.

Data

published

 by the

Guardian

 in early September revealed that American forces and weapons corporations control or make use of over 100 military facilities across the country. And Australia is one of the biggest recipients of US arms in the world, with around 85 percent of weapons purchased in 2021-25 coming from the US,

according

 to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s arms transfers database.

Hegseth himself

recalled

 during a separate love-in event with Marles last year: “We [the Australian and US militaries] fought shoulder to shoulder in every major conflict since World War One—from the Western Front, to Guadalcanal, to Vietnam, to Afghanistan”.

“During my time in Afghanistan”, he reminisced, “I served with members of the Australian military who were some of the finest”. We can only imagine the sorts of unconvicted war criminals who consorted with Pete Hegseth during the joint twenty-year occupation of Afghanistan.

The US alliance has long been a pillar of Australia’s foreign policy, but the current Labor government seems particularly eager to grovel to America. Just one month after Donald Trump’s inauguration, and before the current Australian and US defence ministers had even met for the first time, the Australian government arranged a

payment

 of US$500 million towards the Trump administration’s military budget.

“We’re really pleased that the first payment ... we’ve been able to make in the first couple of weeks of the Trump administration”, Marles told Hegseth ahead of their first formal meeting in February 2025. “We’re really pleased to make it in the first week of your tenure as the secretary of defence.”

In the meeting that followed, Marles

explained

 that Hegseth’s enthusiasm for military ties with Australia made sense, since “the whole idea of a free and open Indo-Pacific really has its origins during the first Trump Administration”.

You wouldn’t be wrong to interpret this behaviour as pathetic bootlicking. The Australian government is a simpering bunch of pro-American lowlifes. But the problem isn’t that our leaders are “weak” or being strong-armed into subservience. They run the twelfth largest economy in the world. Their armed forces outstrip those of any oceanic neighbours by a wide margin. The reality is that Australian capitalism is a willing and culpable participant in the world’s most powerful military coalition alongside America.

As former Labor Prime Minister Kevin Rudd recently

stated

, the “alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs”. With the help of its powerful …

title: Türkiye-Yunanistan gerilimi: Sadece bir sınır sorunu değil emperyalist planda yer kapma meselesi
content:
Seyit Aldoğan [email protected]

Atina- Son dönemde Ortadoğu, Doğu Akdeniz, Ege ve İran ekseninde gelişen ABD-İsrail savaşının yaygınlaşma eğilimi, bir anlamda Türk-Yunan ilişkilerini de tetikledi. Bu durum Türkiye basınında “Atina’da deprem”, “Atina gerilim istiyor”, “Yunanistan ve İsrail ablukası” benzeri manşetlerin atılmasına neden oldu. Karşılıklı restleşmeler, uyarılar ve milliyetçi söylemlerle düşmanlığı körükleyen değerlendirmeler havada uçuşuyor.

Dünyada emperyalist rekabetin kızışmasına, pazar paylaşımı mücadelesine ve emperyalist savaşların yaygınlaşma eğilimi içine girmesine paralel olarak, üzerinde yaşadığımız coğrafyada da enerji nakil hatları, hidrokarbon rezervleri ve deniz taşımacılığı gibi etkenlere bağlı olarak Türkiye-Yunanistan ilişkilerinde yeni bir gerginliğe doğru gidildiği görülüyor.

ABD ve onun bölgedeki vurucu gücü olan İsrail yeni bir yapılanmayı hedeflerken, bölgedeki gerici yönetimler pastadan pay kapmak, emperyalist sistemin bir parçası olarak varlıklarını sürdürmeyi güvence altına almak ve bölgesel çıkar dengeleri içinde daha iyi bir mevzi tutmak amacıyla dış politika, ticaret, silahlanma ve ittifaklarda yeni yönelimler içine giriyorlar. Bölge gericiliklerinin çıkarlarının farklılıklar göstermesi emperyalizme bağımlılıkla çelişmediği gibi, tersine bu bağımlılığı daha da güçlendiren birer etmen haline geliyor.

Bölgedeki gelişmelere bu perspektifle bakıldığında Türkiye ve Yunanistan arasında anlaşmazlık konusu olan sorunların klasik anlamda bir sınır sorunu olmaktan çıktığı açıkça görülecektir.

Rusya Karadeniz, Balkanlar ve Doğu Avrupa’dan abluka altına alınıyor. Yunan adalarına hava savunma sistemlerinin yerleştirilerek Ege kontrol altına alınmaya çalışılıyor. Doğu Trakya ABD-NATO üssüne çevriliyor. Öte yandan Doğu Akdeniz’de İsrail, Güney Kıbrıs ve Yunanistan arasında enerji nakil anlaşmasının yürürlüğe girmesi, Yunanistan’ın münhasır ekonomik bölge çerçevesi içinde uluslararası tekellerle yaptığı anlaşmalar, enerji rezervlerinin önemi, Ortadoğu’ya müdahalede bölgenin önem kazanması, Çin ve Rusya ile girişilen rekabet vb. gelişmeler Türkiye ile Yunanistan arasındaki sorunların artık klasik anlaşmazlıklar olmaktan çıktığını gösteriyor. Gelişmeler, Ege ve Doğu Akdeniz’i emperyalist yayılmacılık, paylaşım ve egemenlik rekabetinin açıkça görüldüğü alan durumuna getiriyor.

Yunanistan’da 1973 yılında yıkılan Albaylar Cuntası sonrasından bugüne kadar kurulan en işbirlikçi yönetim olan Kiryakos Miçotakis’nin Yeni Demokrasi (ND) hükümeti, Ege’de ve Doğu Akdeniz’de Yunan sermayesinin çıkarları doğrultusunda başta ABD, İsrail ve sonrasında AB ile, son derece stratejik anlaşmalar yapmış bulunuyor. Mısır, Lübnan, BAE, Suudi Arabistan ile askeri ve ticari ve teknik ilişkiler geliştirdi. Bu arada özellikle Fransız ve Alman tekellerinin çıkarlarının sözcülüğünü de yapıyor.

Erdoğan hükümeti ise ABD ve AB destekli İsrail, Yunanistan ve Güney Kıbrıs kesimi eksenine karşı Suriye’de sahip olduğu etkiyi, son süreçte Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan ile kurulan “Mekke ittifakı”nı, ABD ve NATO politikaları ile tam bir uyum içinde olan tutumunu; Trump’ın övgüsünü kazanan İran ve Filistin politikasını, NATO politikaları çerçevesi içinde artan silahlanma harcamalarını kullanarak elini güçlendirmeye ve bölge ülkeleriyle kurduğu ekseni güçlendirmeye çalışıyor.

Kuşkusuz her iki ülkenin bağımlılığı daha fazla artıran bu tutumlarının ana nedeni sadece Türk-Yunan ilişkileri ve Ege-Doğu Akdeniz gibi sorunlarla açıklanamaz. Esas neden bölgede oluşan ya da oluşması olası olan dengelerden pay kapma yarışıdır. Türkiye’yi asıl kaygılandıran İsrail’in bölgede oyun kurucu duruma gelme planlarıdır. Örneğin “yavru vatan” ilan edilmesine ramak kalan Suriye’de İsrail’in etkisinin artması ve Colani hükümeti ile anlaşma masasına oturulması, Arap ülkeleriyle İbrahim anlaşmalarının imzalanması, Yunanistan’ın AB üyesi olarak Türkiye ile bölgesel çıkarlar üzerinden iş birliği yapan ülkeler ve tekellerle ekonomik, askeri ve ticari ilişkiler geliştirmesi Türkiye’nin yayılmacı politikaları önünde ciddi engeller oluşturuyor.

Son süreçte ise Yunanistan, Kıbrıs ve İsrail arasında çekilen elektrik hattı ve Türkiye tarafından hazırlanan “Mavi vatan” kanunu ve “deniz parkları” kararı, iki ülke arasında gerginliğin yeniden yükselmesine neden oldu. Yunan hükümeti “Mavi vatan” kanununun “hiçbir geçerliliğinin olmayacağını” savunurken, Dışişleri Bakanı Yorgos Gerapetritis defalarca “Yunanistan her türlü tahrike karşı koymaya hazırdır” …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. Peripheral societies are forced to absorb the crisis through debt traps, budget cuts, declining purchasing power, and reduced national sovereignty. High energy prices further incentivize ruling elites to expand speculative and destructive extraction projects in the name of energy security and geopolitical hegemony.

This energy regime is increasingly bound up with “Pax Silica”—the global alliance centered on microelectronics, semiconductor supply chains, and automated defense systems. Localized military interventions rely on a global network of critical mineral extraction, energy consumption, and defense technology transfer. The fusion of high-tech militarism and fossil capital reinforces imperialist control over global supply lines, shifting the operational costs of planetary warfare directly onto the working classes of the Global South.

At the same time, a “super” El Niño brings the violence of ecological crisis directly to the doorsteps of the global peasantry, smallholders, and urban poor. Although the historical carbon footprint belongs overwhelmingly to the industrial centers of the imperialist world, the physical destruction—manifested in crop failures, severe drought, flooding, and damaged infrastructure—falls disproportionately on semicolonial societies. Framing these events as merely “natural disasters” shields the capitalist mode of production from critique and obscures climate catastrophe as an institutionalized assault on oppressed and economically vulnerable populations.

Far from resolving the agrarian question, this ecological and economic squeeze accelerates what Paris Yeros calls generalized semiproletarianization. In this condition, households that have lost all or part of their means of production do not become fully dependent on wages. Instead, they combine precarious employment with small-scale farming, petty trade, subsistence production, care work, and other sources of livelihood (Yeros, 2023). Across much of the Global South, this blurs the conventional boundary between peasant and worker and produces socially fragmented labor forces that move between rural and urban economies (Moyo & Yeros, 2005; Moyo et al., 2013; Yeros, 2024).

Under conditions of monopoly capitalism, these labor reserves can weaken workers’ bargaining power and shift the costs of social reproduction onto households and communities (Marx, 1976; Yeros, 2023). Millions may circulate between degraded smallholder farming, informal street trade, temporary migration, and precarious wage work without being absorbed into secure urban industrial employment. Rather than representing a simple transition from peasant production to wage labor, semiproletarianization describes a durable social formation in which rural and urban livelihood strategies remain interdependent (Yeros, 2023).

To propose “ecosocialism” as a generic, off-the-shelf alternative to this twin crisis, without subjecting the term itself to critical scrutiny, is to risk reproducing a dangerous conceptual trap. Much dominant Western-centered ecosocialist discourse reduces the problem to an abstract, planet-wide carbon-accounting exercise. In doing so, it can erase the national question, gloss over the unresolved agrarian question, and ignore the necessity of national-liberation struggles in …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

Climate change is the real security threat. Pacific leaders named climate change their main security threat in the 2018 Boe Declaration. Yet Australia keeps expanding fossil fuel exports while spending hundreds of billions on submarines.

But AUKUS is about so much more than submarines; its more sinister part is AUKUS Pillar II, which is about “advanced capabilities” including: undersea capabilities; quantum science; artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy; advanced cyber; hypersonics and counter-hypersonics; and electronic warfare.

Any pretense about “defensive” capabilities is put to rest with Pillar II because these technologies are about highly efficient offensive war-fighting capabilities.

The Australian Human Rights Commission said it is arguably impossible for AI to comply with the proportionality rule, because AI is unable to understand the intrinsic value of human life.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that machines determining proportionality in life-or-death situations is “politically unacceptable and morally repugnant”.

Australia said in 2018 that it was premature to regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems. Nearly a decade later, it maintains this position despite significant advances and uses of the technology.

It is instead barrelling ahead with developing the most advanced and lethal forms imaginable.

The first “signature project” of AUKUS Pillar II was announced in May — payloads and systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles are due from 2027, covering surveillance, reconnaissance, strike, anti-submarine and electronic warfare, among other missions.

The stated aim is meeting near-term war fighting objectives. The Ghost Shark project for Australia is being developed by Silicon Valley-based defence contractor Anduril. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said they will conduct surveillance and can strike at extremely long distances. It means the weapon is designed to operate far from our shores — not for defence.

Pillar II extends into the realms of software and artificial intelligence. Tests for active warfighting scenarios to integrate Australian, British and US AI models have been ongoing for years.

A 2023 pilot had Australia PA-8 Poseidon aircraft sharing data for submarine detection, amid other tests of “AI-enabled assets” and machine-learning models.

There was a large-scale US trial in 2024. The US Department of War was enthusiastic: “These trials demonstrated significant progress since the first AUKUS RAAIT trails in the UK in April 2023 and show tangible results of the AUKUS Pillar II commitment to making our warfighter more lethal on the battlefield.

“It used to be that each nation used its own datasets to develop separate models and deploy those models on their own platforms. Under RAAIT, we’ve matured the AI pipeline, focusing on interchangeability and interoperability, which allows for any combinations of datasets, models, algorithms and platforms to be used across all three nations.”

These models and cloud computational capacity are key to war power investments today.

The Pentagon’s AI office awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to US$200 million each for military and intelligence AI last year.

Remember the dispute between Anthropic and the US Department of War …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: New: “Requiem for French Theory” by Aymeric Monville, Jennifer Ponce de León and Gabriel Rockhill
content:
In the public eye: “Requiem for French Theory”


Coming from Left Field

 (Episode 152)


In this episode of Coming From Left Field, philosopher and cultural critic Gabriel Rockhill joins

Greg Godels & Pat Cummings

 to explore the Ford Foundation, the 1966 Johns Hopkins conference often cited as a launching point for French Theory in the United States, Cold War cultural politics, and the wider political economy of academic knowledge production. Rockhill argues for rebuilding a class-centered, internationalist Marxism and joins a thoughtful exchange on China, Vietnam, socialism, imperialism, inequality, and the challenges of assessing existing socialist projects without demonization or uncritical celebration….


REVIEWS


Marxism-Leninism Today,

 by

Greg Godels

:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful U.S. counterparts—revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism–counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven U.S. New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics–quite often a reconsidered Marx–and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers….”

Read more…


ZZ’s Blog

, as reviewed by Zigedy:


“During the 1960s and 1970s, it was an oft-repeated quip that the European left was long on theory and short on practice, while the North American left was strong on action, but allergic to theory. In West Germany, Italy, and France, young leftists would often passionately debate theoretical questions deep into the night, while seldom coming to a common commitment to action the next day. Their youthful US counterparts–revived after the retreat from High McCarthyism– counted on spontaneous action and a firm commitment to common, inherited political values rather than the ideas buried in deep theoretical tracts. But those observations were far from completely true. The often student-driven US New Left developed a thirst for a broader, deeper explanation of the injustices that they were rejecting. Many of those committed to action turned to left classics– quite often a reconsidered Marx– and others favored a wave of West European radical-oriented thinkers. It is the rise and importation to the US of one particularly influential “brand” of European theory to which Aymeric Monville and Gabriel Rockhill’s new book is devoted.


In

 Requiem for French Theory: Transatlantic Funeral Dirge in a Marxist Key

 (New York,

Monthly Review Press

, 2026, $22.00, 168 pp.), Monville and Rockhill show that what became known as “French Theory” in the US was both a calculated interruption of the rediscovery and study of Marxism and an intellectual trend hostile to anti-capitalist and socialist currents….”


In translation….
